Rashid al-Alimi, the Riyadh-based president of Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, called on Yemenis on Friday to mobilise and join the armed forces.
He also offered a future general amnesty to Houthi fighters and affiliates who leave the group starting 26 September.
The military chiefs of staff of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have finished a meeting in Riyadh to discuss how to respond to the Houthis' ongoing attacks on the kingdom, Ankara said on Friday.
Turkey's defence ministry earlier said its chief of general staff was travelling to Saudi Arabia on Friday to attend the meeting, with Saudi state media also announcing planned military talks but without providing further details.
Later on Friday, Ankara published photographs of the three military officials in uniform, stating that the meeting had taken place, without disclosing where.
The Iran-backed group has escalated its attacks on the kingdom since July, ending a years-long truce and declaring a maritime blockade, hitting Saudi targets and seizing Yemen's entire Red Sea coast as they seek to stifle Saudi oil exports.
Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear programme even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the waterway would remain closed until "all of Iran’s conditions are met" by the United States.
Under Iran’s proposal, Tehran has offered to reopen the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz. Within seven days, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, the United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday.
The proposal follows a sharp escalation in Middle East tensions after seven months of war between Iran and the United States, with Iran-backed Houthi militias in Yemen launching missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.
US President Donald Trump said Friday he had discussed the Iran war with visiting Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, following allegations that Beijing has been supporting Tehran.
"We did, we did," Trump said when asked if they had talked about Iran, as he showed Xi around the National Archives in Washington on the last day of the Chinese leader's state visit.
Asked if he thought there would be progress on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, Trump replied: "I think we're going to do great."
China sent around 1,300 shipments of dual-use components suitable for drones and missiles to Iran in the first half of 2026, according to Iranian customs data seen by The Wall Street Journal.
The components included electronics, GPS devices, electric motors, aircraft-engine parts and other items that can support Iran’s drone programs and missile guidance systems.
One notable delivery arrived in Tehran on 17 June, the same day the US and Iran agreed to a 60-day truce.
Two days later, more than a dozen shipments landed carrying more than $6 million worth of parts usable in drones.
Colombia's new far-right US-backed government said on Thursday it had cut diplomatic ties with Iran based on "hemispheric national security" considerations.
It accused the Iranian government of having ties to "narco-terrorist groups that threaten the security of the country," without giving proof of the allegations.
Iran's foreign ministry hit back on Friday, calling the allegations "baseless claims".
Iraq's Najaf airport, a top destination for Shia pilgrims, suspended all Iranian flights on Friday, enforcing US sanctions and leaving travellers scrambling for solutions.
Airport director Hussein Muhanna told AFP that "all flights were halted between Iran and Najaf airport following a directive from the prime minister's office to the governor" of Najaf.
"All Iraqi airports, including in Kurdistan, have enforced the ban," a government source told AFP.
The airport in the holy city of Najaf, south of Baghdad, is a major hub for Iranian flights and their main destination in Iraq.
They mainly carry Iraqi Shia pilgrims to Iran's holy cities or Iranians visiting sacred sites in Iraq. The flights also serve Iraqi students studying in Iran, and patients seeking medical treatment there.
The United Nations' top official for refugees warned on Friday that conditions for long-displaced people in Western Sahara were getting worse and that their humanitarian needs were starkly underfunded.
Western Sahara, a mineral-rich former Spanish colony, has been largely controlled by Morocco since 1975, but the United Nations considers it a non-self-governing territory.
Morocco has waged a decades-old conflict with the Algerian-backed Polisario Front, which seeks independence for the Sahrawi people.
"In Western Sahara, displacement has persisted for more than half a century," the UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih, himself a former refugee, told the UN Security Council. "Generations of Sahrawi refugees have grown up in Tindouf and camps nearby, facing uncertainty and limited prospects."
The top diplomats of Egypt and Iran met on Friday to discuss resuming peace talks between Tehran and Washington, Egypt's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The foreign ministers discussed "proposals being put forward to reach an agreement that leads to containing tensions and de-escalation", it said.
“[Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr] Abdelatty also underscored the importance of respecting the security and stability of Gulf states and all nations in the region,” the statement added.
The meeting came after Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi submitted a new seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume peace negotiations with the US.
Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam insisted at the UN Friday on the need to "avert the vacuum" that would be caused by withdrawing the UN peacekeeping mission deployed in the south of his country without a viable replacement.
"What we wish to stress here and today is the need to avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it," he said.

articles.title: 'No longer hybrid' — As Russian sabotage grows bolder, Europe lacks red lines
articles.body:
'No longer hybrid' — As Russian sabotage grows bolder, Europe lacks red lines
Soldiers from the 16 Air Assault Brigade set up a mortar firing position after parachuting from a British Royal Air Force A400M transport aircraft onto Salisbury Plain at the Copehill Down training facility near Warminster, England, on March 30, 2026. (Finnbarr Webster/Getty Images)
Moscow's shadow war on Europe grows bolder by the day, and no one can say how far the Kremlin is ready to go.
Russia is no longer only meddling in elections or hacking networks: Germany found explosives-laden drones at its Leipzig Airport in an apparent Moscow-backed sabotage plot. Russian drone incursions in NATO airspace are now common. And a Russian warship shot flares at a Danish military helicopter.
The rhetoric in Western capitals has hardened, with some saying this campaign is "no longer hybrid at all."
For the first time, Berlin named Russia as a perpetrator of a physical attack against its infrastructure, and allies grow less fearful about downing drones and detaining shadow fleet ships.
But even as European officials warn that Moscow's campaign may yet escalate in the coming months, the question of how to deter it remains unanswered.
The response so far has ranged from symbolic ones, like shuttering Russian cultural and diplomatic centers, to fresh sanctions and arms packages for Ukraine — something that Moscow has weathered for years.
Analysts say Europe must toughen up, with some calling for novel ways of retaliation that will catch the Kremlin off guard.
"We've got to make Russia think: 'OK, s**t, they're awake,'" proposes Edward Lucas, a British journalist, security analyst, and head of the Baltic International Security Center (BISC).
read also
Testing Europe
Russian hybrid warfare — from cyberattacks and GPS jamming to disinformation campaigns and election meddling — was nothing new for NATO countries prior to 2022.
But Moscow cranked up its operations to a whole new level after the full-scale war broke out, with its suspected proxies setting warehouses on fire and its shadow fleet allegedly cutting cables and launching drones over strategic targets across Europe.
Researchers say that the number of hybrid attack incidents increased fourfold between 2023 and 2024, with one study recording 151 incidents in Europe between the start of the full-scale invasion and March 2026.
"It is Europe's slow and weak response that allows Russia to keep doing so and trying just "how far it can go."
This campaign has become increasingly kinetic since 2025, when a group of Russian drones invaded Polish airspace. Moscow's drones are now probing other countries at NATO's frontier, from the Baltic to the Black Sea.
Such attacks aim not only to sow panic and disrupt support for Ukraine, but also to test Europe's willingness to hit back, officials and experts say.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned on Sept. 17 that Russia might soon launch further "accidental" missile and drone strikes into NATO's territory to prove that Article 5 "is more theoretical than practical."
Moscow is testing something that Julian Pawlak, a security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), calls a "deterrence gap" — Europe's blank spot between its current response toolkit and a full-on military response against Russia.
And it is Europe's slow and weak response that allows Russia to keep doing so and trying just "how far it can go," the expert told the Kyiv Independent.
Part of the reason European nations are often slow to respond is the difficulty of finding solid evidence that allows them to publicly blame Russia.
Moscow often uses proxies; for example, vulnerable Ukrainian and Belarusian refugees recruited through the Telegram messaging app, says Anastasia Pociumban, an expert in hybrid threats at the German Council on Foreign Relations.
However, Pociumban also believes that the "states often use these delays to avoid taking costly response measures and not to create panic."
NATO made clear already in 2016 that a hybrid attack can trigger Article 5. But it doesn't define what red line the attacker would have to cross — that's up to individual states.
Pawlak raises doubt over whether "European politicians or capitals actually themselves know where this line is."
Adding to that, NATO members may be reluctant to invoke Article 5 at a moment when the alliance grapples with internal divisions, as a lackluster or absent response from allies could shake its credibility.
The U.S. under the Trump administration is shifting away from Europe, while Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico recently declared that his country would not be drawn into a war "because of some Article 5."
And German officials said it is "no coincidence" that fresh cases of sabotage in Germany came shortly before regional elections, which saw major wins for the Kremlin-friendly, NATO-skeptic Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Pociumban sees a "two-front pressure campaign" — with Russia deploying not only physical and cyber attacks but also leveraging parties that want to "normalize" ties with Moscow.
read also
Europe's response
A response to a Russian hybrid attack roughly comes in three steps — countering its impacts, identifying the culprit, and deterring the perpetrator from trying something like this again.
Europe has seen progress in the first area.
NATO air defenses are building up drone defenses along the border and are finally downing Russian drones.
"Europe should "blindside" the Kremlin by the scale and range of its responses."
European navies are stepping up protection of maritime infrastructure and are detaining suspected Russian shadow fleet vessels, and governments are bolstering protection of critical infrastructure.
Countries on the front lines of Russia's hybrid war — such as the Nordics and the Baltics — are further integrating military and civilian defenses, aiming to counter the very kind of threat Moscow's shadow war poses.
Estonia, for example, aims to expand the law enforcement role of military and allied forces to help counter threats similar to the "little green men" scenario in Crimea in 2014, when Russian troops without insignia occupied Ukraine's peninsula.
And European officials are learning not to mince words and talk about Russia's campaign more openly.
The Leipzig Airport attack marked the first time Berlin officially accused Moscow of orchestrating such an attack on its soil.
Estonian Intelligence Chief Kaupo Rosin dismissed "hybrid warfare" as a euphemism and urged European leaders to describe Moscow's campaign as "state-sponsored terrorism."
The stance was echoed by EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas, who said Moscow's campaign bears "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism."
Nevertheless, deterring this campaign is the most persistent problem.
After Germany officially blamed Russia for the Leipzig Airport attack, its response — next to promising additional support for Ukraine — was to shut down a Russian consulate and tighten visa access for Russian citizens.
"You should have done this a decade ago… after (Russia occupied) Crimea in 2014," Lucas told the Kyiv Independent.
Europe must "get on the front foot and take the initiative," he adds.
read also
Deterrence
In 2022, just a few months after the invasion, Lithuania banned the transit of EU-sanctioned goods to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
Russia's threats of "retaliation" sparked concern in Brussels, which in turn pressured Vilnius to relent.
Three years later, Estonia attempted to stop a shadow fleet tanker it said was violating sanctions — before a Russian Su-35 entered NATO airspace to shield the tanker, preventing the boarding.
Tallinn later said it would refrain from detaining shadow fleet ships due to the risk of military response.
The record shows that when smaller front-line states want to take bolder steps, they need solidarity so as not to bear the brunt of Russia's response alone.
This is what Lucas calls a lateral response — if a Russian drone violates Estonian airspace, it could be Sweden, Germany, or the U.K. that hits back.
Analysts agree that Europe must increase the costs to Russia of its hybrid war. But they propose different ways of going about it.
According to Pawlak, Europe should set a clear line and make sure the aggressor knows that if it carries out Action A, Europe will respond with Action B — for example, sending another shipment of arms to Ukraine.
Lucas proposes a different path: Europe should "blindside" the Kremlin by the scale and range of its responses.
A sabotage attack should trigger, for example, "a money-laundering investigation in one jurisdiction, an unseaworthy ship impounded in a second, a cyberattack on a Russia-related target launched from a third," he writes in his April column.
But Europe must be ready to see its response through, even if Moscow escalates, Lucas adds in comments for the Kyiv Independent.
"Because it would be disastrous if we see an initial escalation (by a European country), Russia then threatens, and the (European) country backs down again," he warns.
read also

Hi, this is Martin Fornusek.
I hope you enjoyed this article. In our team, we believe fact-based and truthful reporting should be available to all — that's why we don't use any paywall.
If you want to see more in-depth coverage of regional politics and how it shapes Ukraine's struggle against Russian aggression, please consider joining the Kyiv Independent community.

articles.title: Russia's faster Shaheds could rival ballistic missiles this winter
articles.body:
Russia's faster Shaheds could rival ballistic missiles this winter
Rescue workers put out a fire at a building damaged in a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 25, 2026. (Evgeniy Maloletka / AP)
Oleksiy Moskalenko
Senior Analyst at the Come Back Alive Initiatives Center
A few months ago, the only particularly serious threat to Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities came from Russian and North Korean ballistic missiles.
As the Ukrainian mil-tech industry and air defense units perfected their ability to intercept the common "Shahed" drones (now officially called Geran-2, although Ukrainians stick to the original Iranian name), raising the shoot-down rate to 90–95%, a shortage of anti-ballistic interceptor missiles seemed to be the main issue facing Ukraine in the upcoming winter.
However, in this constant arms race, it was Russia's turn to leapfrog, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to new threats while it tested out possible solutions.
August 2026 showed what the new, faster versions of Shahed can do in terms of damage, leaving ground forces' interceptor drone operators — good enough to catch the previous generation of "Shaheds" — without a job. Temporarily.
The new Shaheds are powered by airplane-like jet engines, which allow them to pass through otherwise densely packed air defense zones at speeds of more than 800 km/h (500 mph).
The older generation of attack drones flew at up to 200 km/h (125 mph), requiring the Ukrainian side to master technology that added just 30 km/h (19 mph) to that speed in order to catch up efficiently. Now Ukraine is forced to leap ahead of its current production capacities to build interceptors that can fly at least 450 km/h (280 mph), so the new drones can be taken down when they turn en route or slow down to save fuel.
Whether new interceptors can effectively catch up with jet engine technology is still unknown. We may be heading back to good old missiles as the key means of air defense.
The coming months will give us an answer. Meanwhile, Russia will keep using both old and new drones, as well as ballistic missiles, in an attempt to force Ukrainians to agree to its demands.
As the country braces for another wartime winter, much of the public conversation about Russian air attacks has centered on ballistic missiles and the shortage of Patriot interceptors needed to stop them. But officials and drone crews say that even a cheaper, more numerous threat of new and old Shaheds may end up doing just as much damage.
Over the summer, Russia noticeably scaled back its drone campaign. According to Ukraine's Air Force, the number of older versions of Shahed/Gerbera drones launched fell by a third in June and July compared to a record-setting May.
Yet Moscow has increasingly relied on jet-powered drones, launching nearly 800 of them in just four days in August 2026.
The main reason for this shift, drone unit members say, is that Ukraine has simply gotten better at shooting down the regular, slower drones.
The vast majority of these drones are intercepted by domestically built interceptors flown by dedicated crews stationed across the country. A radar team spots an incoming Shahed, an interceptor crew launches its own drone to locate and pursue the target, and the operator then has to visually acquire the Shahed through the interceptor's onboard camera, close in from behind, and either ram it or detonate nearby, usually knocking off a wing or engine.
For now, the threat from this previous generation of drones seems to have been rendered largely obsolete, but that appearance may be something of an illusion, since the system has one clear weakness: weather.
Strong wind makes the interceptor hard to control, rain can degrade electronics, radar performance, control link, and, crucially, operators still need to see the target through a camera, since radar can guide them to the right area but cannot perform the final identification and targeting itself; low cloud, fog, or rain make that visual search far harder.
It's telling, in this respect, that some interceptor unit command posts reportedly keep a dedicated screen just for tracking weather conditions.
Ukrainian citizens are gradually starting to associate rainy weather with cheaper, slower Shahed drones: "It is likely that today, as on the previous occasion, the adversary will seek to exploit the poor weather to attack areas west of Kyiv using 'conventional' gasoline-powered Shahed drones," said an adviser to the Defense Minister of Ukraine on a rainy evening.
Russian forces appear to be factoring this in already, according to Ukrainian crews, timing launches and routes for stretches when interceptors are least effective.
That is why the summer drop in slower, gasoline Shahed launches shouldn't be read as a lasting decline in the threat.
As fall brings more fog, lower cloud cover, and worse visibility, the conditions that favor Russian drones and hamper Ukrainian interceptors are set to return, giving Moscow an added reason to lean back on its cheapest, slower strike drones.
That, our respondents argue, is the overall conclusion of the current air war.
Each new stage of the technological race doesn't replace the one before it — it adds another layer to a system that has to be sustained with people, hardware, and infrastructure.
Mobile fire groups remain necessary alongside interceptor drones; slower piston-engine Shaheds will keep flying alongside faster jet-powered ones.
Russian forces regularly adapt their tactics and patterns of drone employment in an effort to improve their effectiveness, e.g., they are known to periodically re-test routes they've previously avoided after taking losses, checking whether Ukrainian defenses along that corridor have weakened — which means any capability Ukraine builds now has to be maintained, not shelved, once a newer one arrives.
For now, jet-powered Shaheds are hunted almost exclusively by scarce, expensive fighter jets and surface-to-air missiles, while dedicated faster interceptor drones are still working their way toward serial production.
While this technological gap remains, Ukraine and its partners need to keep investing in developing the skills and the infrastructure of the teams operating in the domain of air defense.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

articles.title: Zelensky Visits Kyiv Maternity Hospital Struck by Russia as Fresh Attacks Kill 7, Including Israeli Teen
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky on Friday visited a Kyiv maternity hospital damaged during Russia’s Sept. 23–24 overnight ballistic missile attack, as fresh Russian strikes across the capital killed seven people, including a 14-year-old Israeli teen, and wounded dozens.
Zelensky met medical staff, expectant mothers and the mother of a baby boy born during the overnight attack. Patients and staff had taken shelter during the strike, and no one at the hospital was injured.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Writing on social media after the visit, Zelensky said: “Each of you deserves to give birth to your child in peace, without sirens or explosions. And every newborn deserves to begin life in peace. We are doing everything to make this happen as soon as possible.”
The visit came as Russia launched another wave of attacks on Kyiv on Friday, hitting residential buildings, offices and other civilian sites across the capital.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said seven people were killed and dozens wounded in the attacks.
Among those killed was a 14-year-old boy later identified by Israel’s Foreign Ministry as an Israeli citizen. His mother was among those wounded.
Zelensky condemned the strike that killed the teenager as “absolutely savage and sickening” and “devoid of any military logic.”
Attacks continued into Saturday, with Klitschko reporting that a Russian drone struck a private medical facility in Kyiv’s Obolonskyi district.
Putin Accuses Kyiv of Striking Polling Stations: ‘We Were Ready to Resume Negotiations’
Twenty-six patients were inside the clinic. Sixteen were transferred to city hospitals, while three people were injured, two of them seriously, according to the mayor.
A separate Russian drone strike hit an office building in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district. Four people were killed there, while vehicles caught fire in a nearby parking area and the building was damaged.
With explosions again sounding across Kyiv in broad daylight, some residents ran for shelter while others continued walking through the streets, AFP reported.
Alisa Boyko, who lived in one of the damaged high-rises, said Russian forces were seeking to “torment” Kyiv residents so that “everyone is affected, one way or another.”
Another resident, Mykyta Sysoyev, described the attacks as part of a technological race.
“This is a technological race and a technological war,” he said. “Unfortunately, people will suffer while we’re searching for solutions.”
Zelensky Says Trump Approved Patriot Production Licenses
The renewed strikes came days after Zelensky addressed the UN General Assembly in New York and again pressed Ukraine’s partners for stronger air defenses.
During his visit to the United States, Zelensky met US President Donald Trump, with Ukraine’s need for additional air-defense systems among the key issues discussed.
On Friday, Zelensky said Trump had made a “final decision” to allow Ukraine to receive licenses to produce missiles for Patriot air-defense systems.
“At our last meeting, President Trump emphasized to me that yes, I have made a final decision. Ukraine will receive licenses for the production of Patriot missiles,” Zelensky told journalists.
Ukraine has repeatedly sought additional Patriot systems and interceptors as Russia intensifies ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Russian Strikes Hit Civilian Sites Across Ukraine
The attacks were not limited to Kyiv.
In Odesa region, another person was killed in a Russian double-tap strike on a postal facility, according to Zelensky.
In Zaporizhzhia, firefighters and medical workers evacuated seven patients after a Russian drone damaged a hospital and sparked a fire in one of its wards. Two people were injured.
The attacks came as Russian forces continued striking residential areas, transport infrastructure, businesses, logistics facilities and other civilian sites across Ukraine.

articles.title: Zelensky says Trump made ‘final decision’ to give Ukraine Patriot licence
articles.body:
Zelensky says Trump made ‘final decision’ to give Ukraine Patriot licence
- Ukrainian President Zelensky confirmed that US President Trump made the "final decision" to grant Ukraine licences to produce advanced Patriot missiles amid urgent defence needs.
- Kyiv faces a severe shortage of Patriot missiles to counter Russia’s growing drone and missile attacks, with immediate needs unmet despite potential future production.
- A recent Russian drone strike killed a 14-year-old in Kyiv, prompting Zelensky to condemn it as a "savage and sickening strike," highlighting the ongoing civilian suffering and technological warfare.
AI generated
KYIV – Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sept 25 said US President Donald Trump told him he would allow Ukraine to produce advanced Patriot air defence missiles, after a series of reversals on the issue.
Kyiv is facing a shortage of the missiles, needed to counter Russia’s increasing drone and missile attacks on the country, the latest of which killed a 14-year-old boy in the capital on Sept 25.
Zelensky during his latest visit to the United States this week renewed calls for air defence support, and for the Patriots, which remain the only system reliably able to counter Russia’s powerful ballistic missiles.
“At our last meeting, President Trump emphasised to me that yes, I have made a final decision. Ukraine will receive licences for the production of Patriot missiles,” Zelensky said in a voice note to journalists.
In July, Trump said it would be “pretty cool” to grant Ukraine the licences, before backtracking, saying the US should be “very careful” before granting Ukraine authorisation.
Ukraine has reported an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in February, diverting supplies of the advanced systems.
Even if the licences are granted, establishing industrial capacity would require more than a year and would not meet Kyiv’s immediate needs.
And Kyiv, preparing for winter, has renewed calls for urgent support.
It needs 5 per cent of the US’ Patriot interceptor missiles to get through the winter and 10 per cent to destroy all of Russia’s ballistic projectiles, Zelensky said in August.
‘Savage and sickening strike’
Moscow has also been aiming at the capital with newly developed jet-powered drones, which have succeeded in bypassing some of the drone interception systems developed by Ukraine.
While it used to target Kyiv mainly during the hours of darkness, Moscow now often attacks in broad daylight.
As people were making their way to work on the morning of Sept 25, a drone struck a residential building in the city, killing a 14-year-old boy.
Zelensky denounced the attack, calling it “an absolutely savage and sickening strike, devoid of any military logic”.
AFP journalists on the spot saw residents gathering around a multi-storey building, with apartments on the ninth and 10th floors left charred by the attack.
Mykyta Sysoyev was smoking a cigarette outside his damaged building.
The 23-year-old IT specialist said he was woken up by an explosion but only realised the strike had hit his own building when he checked the news.
“My jaw dropped a bit,” he said. “It’s strange: on the one hand, I’ve got used to it, but on the other, people are constantly dying.”
Asked about the increase in drone strikes, he added: “This is a technological race and a technological war... Unfortunately, people will suffer while we’re searching for solutions.”
In the southern region of Odesa, another person was killed in a repeated strike on a postal facility, the authorities said. AFP

articles.title: Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
articles.body:
Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the waterway would remain closed until the United States meets “all of Iran’s conditions.”
According to a US official later on Friday, the United States is having positive, constructive discussions with Iran through mediators and continues to discuss nuclear issues.
Under Iran’s proposal, Tehran has offered to reopen the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz. Within seven days, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon; the United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds, and waive its oil sanctions, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday.
Araghchi reiterated to reporters at the UN on Friday that the “choice rests with the US” to accept and implement Iran’s proposed seven-day plan. The conditions outlined in the plan are not new, he said, as they were already included in the June MoU. He added that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until the plan’s conditions were fulfilled. “Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure,” Araghchi said.
The proposal follows a sharp escalation in Middle East tensions after seven months of war between Iran and the United States, with Iran-backed Houthi militias in Yemen launching missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.
Pezeshkian hopes a deal with Washington can be reached before US midterms
In a meeting with journalists on Thursday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said he hoped a deal with Washington to end the hostilities could be reached before the US midterm elections on November 3.
Tehran said it would be prepared to engage in detailed negotiations over its nuclear program only after its conditions are met by the US.
But the official said Iran would give no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, one of the main US demands.
Israel, the United States and other Western states have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, including pointing to its move to enrich uranium to 60%, far higher than needed for civilian uses and closer to the 90% needed for a weapon. Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons.
The International Atomic Energy Agency estimates that Iran had 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% when Israel and the US attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. How much of that has survived is unclear.
Iranian authorities have said that Iran could agree to dilute its most highly enriched uranium.
In May, Reuters reported that Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a directive that the country's HEU should not be sent abroad, according to two senior Iranian sources.

articles.title: Latvia moves to buy Anduril’s Barracuda cruise missiles
articles.body:
- Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs said Latvia expects to complete the purchase of Anduril's Barracuda long-range cruise missiles after visiting the company.
- He also witnessed the signing of cooperation memoranda involving Latvia's Ministry of Defense and Latvian drone maker Origin Robotics.
Latvia is working to buy Anduril’s Barracuda long-range cruise missiles, President Edgars Rinkēvičs said after visiting the American defense company and meeting its founder, Palmer Luckey.
Rinkēvičs wrote that he looked forward to completing the acquisition of the missiles and to further defense industry cooperation. During the visit he also witnessed the signing of memoranda of cooperation involving Latvia’s Ministry of Defense and Origin Robotics, a Latvian drone maker. Neither Latvia nor Anduril has disclosed which Barracuda version Latvia wants, how many missiles it plans to buy, the price or a delivery date. The terms of the memoranda were not made public.
Barracuda is a family of turbojet-powered, subsonic cruise missiles that Anduril unveiled in September 2024 in three sizes: Barracuda-100, -250 and -500. The largest carries a warhead of more than 45 kg (99 pounds) over 926 km (575 miles). Anduril designed the missiles to be built quickly and in large numbers, and says the three versions share more than 90% of their components. The company claims Barracuda costs about 30% less and takes half the time to produce compared with similar cruise missiles.
The missiles can be launched from fighter jets, helicopters, cargo aircraft, ships and ground launchers. Anduril says they can fly together and split roles on a single mission, with some acting as decoys or scouts while others strike.
Barracuda is moving into large-scale production. In May, the U.S. Department of War signed a framework agreement for Anduril to deliver at least 1,000 surface-launched Barracuda-500Ms a year for three years to the U.S. Army, starting in 2027. In July, Poland’s state-owned defense group PGZ signed an agreement to assemble and later produce the Barracuda-500M at its Military Aviation Works No. 2 plant in Bydgoszcz. PGZ said European production could make the missile eligible for purchase by other EU countries under the bloc’s SAFE defense loan program.
Origin Robotics, based in Riga, builds drones for military use. Its BEAK drone is already in combat service in Ukraine. The company has also developed BLAZE, a briefcase-sized drone interceptor that uses radar and AI-based cameras to find and hit enemy drones on its own after launch.
Latvia borders Russia and Belarus. Its longest-range strike weapon on order is the Army Tactical Missile System, a ballistic missile with a range of about 300 km (186 miles) that Latvia is buying along with six HIMARS launchers under a deal approved by the U.S. State Department in 2023. The Barracuda-500 would give Latvian forces roughly three times that reach.

articles.title: EU defense agency says Europe is rearming too slowly to be ready to defend against Russia by 2030
articles.body:
EU defense agency says Europe is rearming too slowly to be ready to defend against Russia by 2030
The EU is not rearming quickly or effectively enough to be ready to defend itself against Russia by 2030, according to a summary of a report prepared by the European Defense Agency for the bloc’s leaders and seen by Reuters.
EU leaders commissioned the report last year to assess progress in strengthening Europe’s defenses. Amid concerns about Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and Donald Trump’s calls for Europe to take on more responsibility for its own security, they set a goal of making Europe ready to defend itself by 2030.
But European countries’ current plans “do not seem to meet” the goal of closing gaps in areas including air and missile defense, ground combat, naval forces, ammunition stockpiles, and drones, the European Defense Agency says.
“Tackling the challenges of a contested and deteriorating security environment and the threat posed by Russia’s aggression requires moving further and substantially faster than now to reach defense readiness by 2030,” the report says.
The summary cites progress in EU defense spending, capability development, and industrial readiness. Even so, “the current momentum and increased investment do not yet translate into sufficiently deployable, sustainable and interoperable forces,” it says, and “critical capability gaps remain.” “What has been achieved so far, although unprecedented, is not yet enough,” the report’s authors say.
EU defense ministers are expected to discuss the European Defense Agency’s report in Brussels on Monday, September 28, before it goes to the bloc’s leaders for consideration.
Ukraine
Russia has stepped up strikes on Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications facilities, the Financial Times reports. The strikes have disrupted internet service in Kyiv and raised concerns among Ukrainian officials that Moscow is trying to undermine Ukraine’s digital economy.
In recent days, Russian forces have struck infrastructure belonging to the internet providers Pavutyna, Etherlink, Crazy Network, and Utels, as well as the hosting companies Cityhost and MiroHost. Data centers in Kyiv have also come under attack. One was in a complex that housed Volodymyr Zelensky’s campaign headquarters in 2019.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces struck the “Kyivstar” and “Parkovyi” telecommunications centers overnight on September 24, claiming they provide “communications services and computing capacity for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”
According to Ukraine’s Digital Transformation Ministry, strikes on September 23 and 24 temporarily left about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region without internet access.
Ukraine’s national communications commission warned of “temporary disruptions to networks and access to telecommunications services.” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the strikes had also disrupted attack alerts sent to mobile phones.
Ukrainian officials and company executives warn that Russia may be trying to cause wider outages that could threaten the digital infrastructure used by banks, online payment providers, businesses, government services, and the military.
The Financial Times notes that, unlike strikes on individual communications networks, an attack on a data center can affect large numbers of users at once if a single facility is damaged.
The war in photos: Russia’s latest strike on Kyiv
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Trump and Chinese president Xi end summit without major agreement on AI
articles.body:
Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping wrapped up their Washington summit on Friday, facing criticism that they had squandered an opportunity to pause their countries’ artificial intelligence (AI) arms race.
The three-day state visit emphasised pageantry and personal rapport rather than substantial agreements. The US president and Xi discussed the wars in Iran and Ukraine and the status of Taiwan. Their biggest policy announcement was a modest two-month extension of a trade truce.
But despite the presence of top tech executives at a White House state dinner on Thursday night, Trump and Xi failed to deliver the AI breakthrough that some experts and foreign governments had hoped for amid warnings that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity.
“It was such a layup,” said Ro Khanna, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives’ select committee on China. “If [Trump] had just said, look, we have established technical working groups and we’ve agreed to a framework that has called for DeepSeek and Moonshot and Alibaba to sit down with Anthropic and OpenAI and Gemini and with technical experts and they’re going to commit to at least a pause on any self-improving AI, he could have looked like he was a statesman taking the lead.
“I believe Xi Jinping would have agreed to some of at least the technical working groups. But he [Trump] didn’t want to; he has no interest in doing that.”
It was the first visit to the White House by a Chinese president in more than a decade and Xi’s second state visit to the US. Three days of pomp and circumstance culminated on Friday with Trump and Xi drinking tea. Trump said the summit had produced great strides and that “our farmers are going to be happy,” but did not provide details.
The pair then went to the National Archives, where Trump and Xi looked at the original Declaration of Independence, the constitution and Bill of Rights. Trump told reporters they were comparing China’s documents to America’s founding documents. “Ours goes 250 years, which is great, and we’re proud of. Theirs goes 6,000 years. So there’s a little difference between 6,000 and 250. But we’re very proud of our 250.”
On Thursday, Xi acknowledged that the US and China have the “responsibility to develop and manage AI for good” and “ensure that the development of AI is always under human control”. China aims to have next-generation smart terminals and AI agents reach more than 90% penetration by 2030.
But Trump – who has repeatedly said the US must forge ahead to maintain its lead over China – appeared more focused on his push to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence”, later claiming on social media that Xi “seems to like” the term without divulging the substance of their discussions.
Later Trump hosted a black-tie state dinner attended by titans of the tech industry. Bernie Sanders, an independent senator of Vermont, used social media to label a photo of Trump and Xi’s table with guests’ net worth: Elon Musk of SpaceX and Tesla ($928bn), Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ($3.5bn), Jensen Huang of Nvidia ($186bn) and Tim Cook of Apple ($3.1bn). Sanders commented: “A government of, by and for the billionaire class.”
But their counterparts in the Chinese tech industry were not present and there was little sign of either country making even a symbolic gesture to apply the brakes.
Khanna commented: “Trump didn’t have to have some groundbreaking treaty like Reagan and Gorbachev did [on nuclear weapons]. He could have at least said, look, we’re going to have a working group of Chinese and American technologists working together to make recommendations and enforcement and verification of the labs.”
Jonathan Czin, a fellow in the China Center at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, agrees that an opportunity was missed. “We are in this potentially transformative moment for both countries and for the world and for technology and, instead of having a meeting that would meet the moment, you got theatre of the absurd in lieu of that,” he said.
“Even going into this meeting, you’re dealing with a septuagenarian and octogenarian who may or may not have ever had first-hand contact with actually using AI and what happens with this technology rests on their two shoulders. The only thing they seemed to agree about is that neither of them wants to slow down with this technology, regardless of their actual understanding of it.”
The state visit underlined the contrast between Trump’s treatment of democratic allies such as Canada and authoritarian rivals such as China. He broke from tradition to give Xi a red carpet welcome when he landed at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
He also found time to show Xi around the White House, including a gallery wall of presidents where Joe Biden is mockingly depicted as an autopen, a construction site for his White House ballroom and a new helicopter landing pad. “He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite,” Trump said.
But the summit was somewhat overshadowed by Trump’s decision last week to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, sparking a legal fight. On Thursday, Chinese state media were welcomed into the White House grounds even as members of America’s free press were frozen out, though later they gained entry. As in May, when Trump visited Beijing, the leaders did not hold a press conference.
Czin of the Brookings Institution added: “I had very low expectations going into this meeting for anything of substance and the meeting managed to underwhelm even those low expectations. We went from the mezzanine down into the basement. In terms of the substance, it’s not clear to me what the US got out of this.”
Senate Democrats also criticised the summit, arguing that Trump failed to secure meaningful concessions from Beijing on trade, security, human rights or AI.
Chuck Schumer, the minority leader in the Senate, said: “As usual, Trump acts based solely on who flatters him at the moment, where the nearest photo op is, and what headline he covets. If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll greet you plane-side.”
Trump and Xi are on track to meet twice more this year. In November, Xi will host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, and in December the Group of 20 summit will be held at the Trump National Doral Miami golf club in Florida.

articles.title: Chinese copy of Russia’s Tor air defense system seen in Algerian colors
articles.body:
- Photos on Chinese social media show an HQ-17 air defense system in camouflage matching Algerian equipment, with Chinese sources saying it is for Algeria.
- Neither Algeria nor China's CASIC has confirmed a sale, and the quantity and delivery date remain unknown.
A Chinese HQ-17 short-range air defense system painted in camouflage matching Algerian military vehicles has appeared in photos shared widely on Weibo, with Chinese sources claiming the system is headed to Algeria.
The photos were highlighted by an OSINT defense account, which noted that the camouflage pattern matches the paint used on a large number of Chinese-made weapons already in Algerian service. The other sources acknowledged a small possibility that the vehicles belong to an export order for a country in Africa’s Sahel region that uses similar camouflage. It also said reports that Algeria operates the HQ-17 had circulated before.
The HQ-17 is a Chinese development of the Russian Tor-M1, a mobile system that detects, tracks and fires on low-flying threats from a single vehicle. China bought 27 Tor-M1 systems from Russia in two contracts in 1996 and 1999, then developed its own version. CASIC built it to shoot down aircraft, helicopters and drones as well as cruise missiles, guided bombs and air-to-surface missiles.
Each launch vehicle carries its own radar and eight missiles, so it can fight without support from other units, though it can also take targeting data from separate surveillance radars. The Chinese version uses an electronically scanned radar designed to resist jamming. The missile reaches Mach 3 and can engage targets between 1.5 km and 20 km (1 to 12 miles) away, at altitudes up to 10 km (33,000 feet).
The People’s Liberation Army Ground Force operates the tracked HQ-17 and the wheeled HQ-17A, which rides on a 6×6 truck and can fire while moving. China first showed an export version, the FM-2000, at the 2018 Zhuhai Airshow and cleared a variant called the HQ-17AE for export in 2021. The HQ-17AE can guide four missiles against four targets at the same time. Serbia operates the HQ-17AE, and the system has also been reported in Saudi Arabia and Tajikistan.
Algeria runs one of the largest air defense networks in Africa, built on both Russian and Chinese equipment. Its long-range layer reportedly includes Russian S-300PMU-2 and S-400 systems alongside the Chinese HQ-9, with Russian Buk-M2 systems at medium range. Algeria has also fielded Chinese CHL-906 electronic warfare vehicles, which its Ministry of National Defense showed during an exercise in the country’s southwest.
A short-range system such as the HQ-17 would sit at the bottom of that network, protecting units and key sites from drones, helicopters and incoming missiles that get past the longer-range layers.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Mirage had killed a cruise missile on its first combat sortie. France just sent more of the missiles that reach 80 km
articles.body:
France delivered additional MICA air-to-air missiles and 30mm cannon ammunition for Ukraine's Mirage 2000 fighter jets, Militarnyi reported, citing France's Armed Forces Ministry.
Delivering an aircraft is one step, keeping it armed is another. France's weapons resupply reflects a shift from one-off hardware transfers to sustained combat support as Russia's aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities grinds on.
What MICA does
The MICA, developed by MBDA, comes in two versions: radar-guided (MICA RF) and infrared (MICA IR). It weighs about 112 kg, flies at Mach 4.9—nearly five times the speed of sound—and can engage targets 60 to 80 km away.
Ukraine's Mirages have also carried older Magic 2 missiles limited to roughly 20 km. MICAs were reportedly included with the original donation, but the supply may have been limited, which would explain why the Magic 2s stayed in use. MICA triples to quadruples that engagement window, letting pilots intercept cruise missiles far earlier in their flight path. The fresh delivery keeps Ukraine's small fleet supplied with the missiles that make these longer-range interceptions possible.
Ukraine is running short of its best missiles for hunting Russia’s jet drones. Now MiG-29s are firing 1970s weapons
Cheap shells for cheap drones
The 30mm ammunition feeds the Mirage's two built-in DEFA 554 cannons, which fire at a selectable rate of 1,200 or 1,800 rounds per minute. A pilot who uses the gun on a Shahed drone saves a MICA for a target that actually needs one.
Ukraine's F-16 operations follow a similar logic: pilots use their 20mm Vulcan cannons alongside AIM-9 and AIM-120 missiles, though Zelenskyy called the missile option expensive—used when nothing else can reach a jet drone, because "a human life is more important."
A Ukrainian Mirage 2000 shot down a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile during its very first combat mission, on 7 March 2025. France has delivered about a dozen modified Mirage 2000-5F jets since February 2025, and the fleet is still growing.

articles.title: Britain’s rhetorical war, Zelensky’s UN crashout, deep state media exposed: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
Britain’s rhetorical war, Zelensky’s UN crashout, deep state media exposed: RT stories that shaped the week
Britain turns up the war rhetoric
Anyone paying the slightest attention to the news this week could be convinced that the UK is preparing for a direct and imminent war with Russia. Retired generals are telling the public to get “psychologically prepared” for conflict; Labour Party thought leaders are suggesting that dissidents and Russia sympathizers be “locked up;” and former Brexit Minister Jacob Rees-Mogg is openly telling British men and women that they “may have to die” – right after calling the English a “mongrel race” with no historic claim to their own homeland.
Meanwhile, Sky News premiered the first episode of ‘The Wargame’ on Monday – a bizarre reality show in which real politicians and military chiefs game out a hypothetical Russian invasion for the cameras.
With the threat from Russia rising in the real world, a new series from Sky brings together former ministers and military chiefs to test what might happen if the UK faced an attack.
Watch the new TV Show 'Wargame' on Sky and NOW from 21 September pic.twitter.com/b9RcuqLHwF
“Britain’s elites,” RT columnist Tarik Cyril Amar concluded, “want you ready to die for a war they keep imagining.”
Talking heads on the continent were equally hysterical, with Spain’s El Mundo claiming that Russia could launch drones at France, Italy, or Spain from ships in the Mediterranean. The fact that the report cited Lithuania’s fanatically anti-Russian government – which in turn cited the CIA – should have been the first sign something was amiss.
It took Finnish President Alexander Stubb to step in as the voice of reason, stating on Wednesday that there is “no imminent military threat right now” from Russia. French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto followed suit on Thursday, with Crosetto declaring that El Mundo’s story “serves no one” and only adds “fuel on the fire.”
President Vladimir Putin has stressed that Russia has no interest in war with NATO. The UK’s escalation remains rhetorical for now: The British military is in no way prepared to wage war, and nobody in London has ordered extra forces to Eastern Europe. If war were to break out, however, it’s not clear whether the UK could count on the US to join in. As RT explored on the weekend, Europe takes on all the risks and costs of fighting Russia under NATO’s new ‘NATO 3.0’ doctrine.
UN-diplomatic behavior
For Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, this week’s UN General Assembly was an opportunity to demand more from his Western backers: more money, more weapons, and more sanctions on Russia.
Asked whether he’d travel to Moscow for peace talks, however, Zelensky said he’d only visit the Russian capital “on a f**king missile.”
Zelensky DOES answer reporters asking when he’ll be heading to Moscow for talks
He COMPLETELY loses his temper as he walks away:
'On a f*cking missile' https://t.co/poqL8qA9Ffpic.twitter.com/f01pupjrnG
In what’s become a familiar pattern, Ukrainian forces hammered Moscow with waves of attack drones on Sunday morning, before Zelensky arrived in New York to plead for a ceasefire ahead of Russia’s inevitable retaliation. Backed by 51 of its allies, Kiev demanded an “immediate and unconditional ceasefire,” which Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov promptly refused.
“We are not going to have a pause in our special military operation,” Lavrov told the UN Security Council. “Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause and it wants to use it to pump the Kiev regime with weapons.”
A tale of two elections in Russia and Germany
Zelensky’s weekend drone attack, deemed “unprecedented” by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, tageted voting in Russia’s State Duma election, but it did little to suppress turnout, which hit a one-decade high of 57%. Putin’s pre-election appeal to patriotism translated into a bump in support for his United Russia party, which went from 49% to 58% of the vote, followed by the Communists and Liberal Democrats.
Curiously, as political scientist Vladimir Kornilov noted for RT, Kremlin-watchers in the West called the election “rigged,” but only after the wave of protest votes against United Russia which they had promised never materialized.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, however, suffered the full wrath of the German electorate over the weekend, as his Christian Democrats (CDU) suffered a historic loss to the right-wing AfD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and trailed the Left Party in Berlin. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a former CDU stronghold and home of ex-Chancellor Angela Merkel’s district, Merz’s party failed to meet the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
“The CDU will never again win a federal election,” AfD co-leader Alice Weidel vowed after the results came in, declaring the AfD “the new people’s party in Germany.”
Exposing the deep state media
Germany’s mainstream parties – the CDU and Social Democrats – have dominated the country’s postwar political landscape. Meanwhile, one name has dominated German media: Axel Springer.
The company bearing Springer’s name stirred some controversy on Thursday when it presented its annual award to Palantir founder Peter Thiel, a name synonymous with the rise of the Silicon Valley military-tech industrial complex. However, as RT explored in our ‘Wired for War’ series, Axel Springer and Palantir are cogs in the same machine: Both took funding from the CIA, and both serve the same globalist order.
The connections between the Western deep state and the mainstream media run deep, and it’s this murky world that RT America’s Ben Swann and independent investigative journalist Elizabeth Lane expose in their brand new series, ‘America Now: Exposing The Deep State of Media.’
Across four episodes, Swann and Lane lift the lid on NATO’s online propaganda machine, the UK’s efforts to frame dissent as disinformation, and the Ukrainian government operation recruiting US military veterans as propaganda agents.
Propaganda goes hand-in-hand with censorship, and it’s the latter field that the EU excels in. While Springer and the covert campaigns uncovered by Swann and Lane shape pro-Western narratives, Brussels uses its Digital Services Act (DSA) to force online platforms to stifle alternate viewpoints. This week, the European Commission published dozens of reports by tech firms including Meta and TikTok, detailing the censorship measures these companies are adopting in order to comply with the DSA. The reports lay bare persistent election interference, collaboration with EU-approved ‘fact-checkers’, and the removal of millions of politically-inconvenient posts.
‘Russia’s Starlink’
Ukraine’s use of SpaceX Starlink broadband service has been instrumental in keeping its forces in the fight for four years. Elon Musk’s portable Starlink terminals allow Ukrainian forces to guide drones to their targets, connect to NATO headquarters, and receive real-time updates from Palantir’s battlefield management software.
It’s an advantage that Russia has worked hard to neutralize with its own Rassvet satellite network. This week, Russian journalist Evgeny Balakin took a deep dive into the Rassvet project and discovered why the Ukrainians are desperate to destroy these satellites on the ground, before they change the balance of power in space.
What we didn’t cover: Negotiating the deepfake
Stories of corruption and graft from Ukraine are legion and unsurprising – we’ve covered a series implicating Zelensky’s inner circle in depth here – but when a video emerged purportedly showing agents with Ukraine’s Western-funded anti-corruption body, NABU, apparently seizing $140 million in cash from former defense procurement chief Arsen Zhumadilov, we took a closer look.
The video was posted on Wednesday, on what initially appeared to be the New Voice of Ukraine’s English-language website. It showed refrigerator boxes stuffed with $100 bills, with an attached note stating that they were for “the servant of the people” – a reference to Zelensky’s political party.
The New Voice of Ukraine was founded by Dragon Capital, whose CEO, Thomas Fiala, is a majority shareholder in Ukrainska Pravda. The latter publication has reported extensively on corruption in the corridors of power in Kiev, and it is believed that Fiala’s position on the board of the Association of European Business (AEB) in Ukraine offers his publications cover to run these controversial stories.
However, the website to which we traced the article carrying the cash claims was dressed-up to look like New Voice of Ukraine, but used a different URL to the actual English-language New Voice of Ukraine site. We held off, correctly, and NABU confirmed on Friday that it had not raided Zhumadilov’s office. “This video is a fake, created using AI,” the agency stated. The New Voice of Ukraine said that the video had been published on an imposter site, attributing the fake to unnamed “Russians.”
There are and will be many “State of Corruption” stories to report on, factually, as the veil is lifted on Zelensky’s regime. But as we’ve learned from the Ukrainian Defense Ministry using video game footage to fake combat victories, and from the Western politicians who fell for the ‘Ghost of Kiev’ hoax, in an era of escalating rhetoric, deep state and deep fake, always double-check your sources.

articles.title: US arms sales to Israel surge to $21.6 bn in 20 months
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US arms sales to Israel worth $21.6 billion in 20 months
Notifications submitted by the US President Donald Trump administration to Congress, along with US State Department data covering the period from 20 January 2025 to 17 September 2026, show that the Trump administration has approved arms deals for Israel worth $21.6 billion in just 20 months.
The value of military aid, funded by US taxpayers, and arms deals approved by former President Joe Biden for Israel between October 2023 and early 2025 exceeded $17.9 billion, according to a study by Brown University.
These weapons were used in the genocide in Gaza and the killing of more than 50,000 civilians, children and women during this period.
September 2026: $2.8 billion in weapons
The US State Department informally notified the offices of the four top Republican and Democratic members in the House of Representatives and Senate last week of a $2.8 billion military aid deal involving new weapons for Israel that Washington is preparing to conclude.
The deal includes 40,000 2,000-pound bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrating warheads.
A 2,000-pound bomb is considered one of the most destructive munitions in the world, as its explosion sends metal fragments thousands of feet in all directions and can penetrate metal and thick concrete.
Despite opposition from Democrats, the deal is expected to pass as usual under emergency authority that allows the administration to bypass congressional objections.
Historically, Congress has failed to stop any arms deal.
The following are the main previous large deals:
January 2025: $2.04 billion
After the Biden administration had previously sent shipments of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel, and as criticism mounted following their use in the genocide in Gaza and the killing of tens of thousands of children and women, his administration suspended one shipment in 2024.
In the first week of the Trump administration after his return to the White House in January 2025, he announced the immediate lifting of the ban on that shipment.
The shipment was valued at $2.04 billion.
February 2025: $7.4 billion
In the first week of February 2025, the US State Department informed Congress in two separate statements that it had approved an arms deal for Israel worth $7.4 billion.
It included 20,000 bombs, guidance systems and equipment worth $6.75 billion, and 3,000 Hellfire air-to-ground missiles worth $660 million.
The administration bypassed congressional notification to obtain approval.
The Trump administration used emergency powers that allow for immediate sales, citing national security interests, to bypass the usual congressional review procedures.
It provided Israel with a $675 million deal including 5,000 1,000-pound bombs and guidance kits and a $295 million deal including Caterpillar bulldozers.
The deal was announced at a value of $3.01 billion, but it included what the administration had announced in January 2025.
June 2025: $510 million
Following the US-Israeli attack on Iran in June 2025, and to rebuild Israel's stockpile, the Trump administration approved the provision of high-precision guidance systems to the Israeli military, worth $510 million.
The deal included more than 7,000 guidance kits for offensive munitions.
January 2026: $6.67 billion
In September 2025, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing sources, that the Trump administration was seeking congressional approval for an arms deal with Israel worth more than $6 billion.
The deal would be funded through the Foreign Military Financing programme, or military aid.
In January, the deal was announced with a total value of $6.67 billion. It includes 30 Apache helicopters, doubling Israel's fleet of this type of aircraft, 3,250 assault vehicles and other equipment.
March 2026: $650 million
One week after the US-Israeli war on Iran began this year, Israel requested more than 20,000 bombs.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, as stated in a statement in March 2026, determined that an emergency existed requiring the sale to Israel to be completed immediately and the deal to be exempted from congressional review.
The deal was announced at a value of $650 million and included 12,000 1,000-pound bombs, as well as 500-pound bombs.
Reuters also quoted an official as saying that Israel would purchase an additional $298 million worth of munitions through direct sales.
May 2026: $992 million
On 1 May, Rubio again used emergency powers to approve a deal for Israel to purchase 10,000 APKWS laser-guided rocket systems worth $992.4 million.
These rockets have been used as countermeasures against Iranian drones because of their lower cost compared with expensive weapons.
This means that the total value of the deals announced and approved by the administration so far is $19.2 billion.
It will rise to $21.6 billion when the administration completes procedures for the latest deal, with at least half of the amount being military aid funded by US taxpayers.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukraine Speeding Up Production of Air Defenses Against Jet-Powered Shaheds
articles.body:
Ukraine is accelerating production of air defense systems capable of countering Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones, which are significantly harder to intercept due to their ability to reach speeds of up to 400-600 kilometers per hour (250-370 miles per hour).
President Volodymyr Zelensky made the announcement on Friday, Sept. 25, after chairing a meeting of Stavka.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“In line with these [Russian] threats, we are adjusting our countermeasures,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky officially formed Stavka on Feb. 24, 2022 – the day Russia launched its full-scale invasion – by signing a decree No. 72/2022 “On the Formation of the Headquarters of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief.”
It brings together the country’s top military commanders, intelligence and security chiefs, alongside key government ministers to make strategic decisions regarding the war.
Russia’s techplans for 2027
During the meeting, officials reviewed test results, the interception rates achieved and the experience of the units carrying out the intercepts.
According to Zelensky, Stavka also made new decisions on setting up production lines in Ukraine for various types of jet engines. He, however, did not specify which air defense had been selected nor did he disclose the interception rates from the tests.
Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) provided Zelensky with a detailed briefing on Russia’s “technological plans” for 2027.
Russian Strikes Hit Ukraine’s Leading Textile Manufacturer and Other Civilian Businesses
The report covered Moscow’s production capacity, the weapons systems it is counting on, as well as the schemes it uses to bypass Western sanctions and bring components into the country.
On Tuesday, the EU agreed to extend sanctions on Russia for three years rather than the usual six to twelve months, under the compromise of removing two Russian oligarchs from the blacklist – Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman – both closely linked to Moscow’s war effort and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Latvia and Estonia responded by imposing national sanctions on both men, while the UK criticized the EU’s move and said it intends to keep their sanctions.
Meanwhile, Ukraine continues preparing for its fifth winter of Russia’s strikes on its critical infrastructure, including the power grid and water supplies, by securing Patriot interceptors from its Western allies.
Earlier on Friday, Zelensky said US President Donald Trump made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine licenses for domestic Patriot production.
Stavka also adopted additional measures to protect data centers and other facilities essential to communications. The aim is to keep them running without interruption, as Russia had increased its campaign on the communications infrastructure, causing disrupted internet access nationwide.
“These decisions must be fully implemented at all levels, and this is the personal responsibility of government officials and heads of the security services,” Zelensky said.
