articles.title: Four years after Russia’s wartime exodus began, another wave may be starting. Political scientist Margarita Zavadskaya on what we’ve learned about Russian emigration since 2022.
articles.body:
Four years after Russia’s wartime exodus began, another wave may be starting. Political scientist Margarita Zavadskaya on what we’ve learned about Russian emigration since 2022.
In 2026, Russians are once again leaving the country en masse. For them, the long process of building a new life almost from scratch is only beginning. Meanwhile, many emigrants have already lived in several countries — and still haven’t found a place to settle down. Others have found a genuine new home, while still others have returned to Russia. Meduza spoke with political scientist Margarita Zavadskaya, a senior research fellow at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs and one of the co-founders of the OutRush project, which studies Russian emigration, about adapting to life abroad, the conflict between “those who left” and “those who stayed,” and the differences between the various waves of emigration.
— How do you generally feel about the discourse around “those who left” and “those who stayed”? Sometimes it seems like this conflict exists only on social media.
— This trope is useful to Russian propaganda, which deliberately promotes it: the idea that those who left are traitors. But there’s also resentment in it from people who don’t support the war and the regime but, unlike “those who left,” are forced to stay in Russia or can’t afford to emigrate. It’s quite possible they feel their compatriots abandoned them. Or they want to stay and consider that the right decision.
The Levada Center asked people how they feel about “those who left,” though those questions were specifically about celebrities. For example, they asked how you feel about Alla Pugacheva. And the poll shows there’s some negativity, but it doesn’t reflect the full picture. The number of people in Russia who have someone who left the country is very small, and it’s hard to dislike someone you’ve never met in your life. So I don’t think there’s really a big rift. But the insidious thing is that even by discussing this narrative, by giving it attention, we’re effectively helping it gain traction.
— How are people outside Russia experiencing this disconnect? Do they feel increasingly removed from what’s happening in Russia and from their loved ones there? After all, things are changing very quickly: drone attacks, fuel shortages, and so on.
— Unfortunately, I don’t have data recent enough to assess how the drone attacks and the fuel crisis have affected relationships within families. But if we look further back, since Russia had gone through upheavals before, those who left tend to feel more empathy toward those who stayed than the other way around. It’s a kind of emotional asymmetry. One of the recent studies from 2026, which I worked on and where I interviewed participants, shows there’s no aggression toward those who stayed. On the contrary, people miss them, want to stay in touch, and regularly keep in contact not only with family members but with friends too.
— Based on your data, do emigrants tend to read news from Russia more or less over time?
— There’s a sense that people are getting more irritated and tired. By 2023, even before Alexey Navalny’s death, many were already complaining that they were sick of reading the news. But few decide to step out of the Russian-language media space entirely.
Everyone is tired of depressing news, and the media are responding to that demand. More entertainment-oriented, quasi-political content is appearing, such as [the show on the independent Russian broadcaster TV Rain] Drama Queens.
— How many people have you surveyed during your research?
— At the start of the [full-scale] war, several colleagues and I co-founded the OutRush project, which has used questionnaires to survey a total of about 18,000 respondents who left Russia after February 24, 2022.
The sample of respondents isn’t representative, but that’s a problem with all migrant studies, including in countries with advanced statistics and immigrant tracking. That’s because it’s hard to determine where the boundaries of diasporas lie. That is, who counts as part of the Russian-speaking diaspora — in Germany, for example, where there are “late repatriots”, who receive German passports right away but in practice often remain within the Russian-speaking community? All existing studies obviously have sampling biases. Ours skews more liberal, more antiwar.
— Do you distinguish waves in Russian migration after 2022?
— I’d say those are fairly loose categories. Personally, I’m not a fan of dividing people into “Septembrists” [those who left when mobilization began] and “Februarists.” It’s as if there’s a moral hierarchy built into it: we’re the real emigrants, who left before the state wanted to claim our bodies, while those who left in September are somehow defective. That’s the wrong way to frame the question, especially for a researcher. Besides, many people left for ideological reasons after September as well.
— But right now there’s a lot of talk about a “new wave of migration” amid rumors of mobilization. Is that reasoning justified? Will we see a major outflow of people this fall?
— There are indeed grounds to talk about heightened readiness to emigrate right now. But I’d separate a simple rise in the desire to leave from an actual mass outflow that has already occurred. Right now we’re seeing a lot of indirect signs of the former. For example, Kovcheg reports that it received almost eight times more inquiries in August than in May. But there are still no lines at the borders and no shortage of tickets to visa-free countries. So anxiety and readiness to leave have clearly grown, but it’s not yet on the scale of 2022.
Right now we’re dealing with rumors of a possible mobilization, not an announced one. Russian authorities publicly deny having such plans. The conditions for a new wave of emigration have formed, but its scale will depend heavily on whether a new, sharp trigger occurs.
A “wave” isn’t just the moment when everyone on social media starts discussing emigration. For a researcher, several independent indicators need to align. The first is intent: search queries, inquiries to organizations that help with relocation, demand for consultations with migration lawyers, interest in renting housing and working abroad. The second is actual movement: border crossings, the number of Russians entering Armenia, Georgia, Kazakhstan, and other countries, airline ticket sales. And the third is “putting down roots” in the new place: applications for residence permits and other legal statuses, enrolling children in school, registering businesses, employment, long-term rentals. The OECD also recommends combining official statistics with digital and other real-time sources when forecasting migration.
How difficult is it to emigrate in 2026
— How is emigration in 2026 different from emigration in 2022? It feels like the reasons now aren’t quite the same as before. In February 2022, the reasons were primarily ethical, while during the mobilization, it was fear for one’s life. Now it seems more like accumulated fatigue: internet censorship, the gasoline crisis, problems with Wildberries, and new strikes.
— There’s actually a fairly significant difference here. That said, I wouldn’t describe February 2022 too rigidly as purely a “moral” emigration. Even then the reasons were mixed: rejection of the war, fear of political consequences, companies and jobs closing, the breakdown of established professional networks, uncertainty about the future (this is visible in OutRush’s early data from the first months of the [full-scale] war). September 2022, on the other hand, really was a much more unambiguous shock: for a great many men, there was suddenly a direct risk of ending up at war.
By 2026, emigration looks more like one driven by accumulated risk: four and a half years of war, internet restrictions, a worsening economic situation, problems with familiar services, drone attacks, a sense of closing opportunities, and, on top of that, rumors of mobilization. So I wouldn’t say there’s less fear now.
There’s another difference from 2022 as well. Over these years an emigration infrastructure has already emerged: people have friends and relatives abroad, Telegram chats, guides, experience from previous attempts to relocate, and a sense of prices and countries.
— Is it easier for people leaving now than for those who emigrated in 2022?
— Any migration is stressful, but it’s also, to some extent, a story about privilege, if we’re talking about a decision to emigrate on one’s own rather than situations where people were literally evacuated.
First, you need to know that you’re welcome wherever you’re going; second, you need to know how to get the paperwork done; third, you need money for it. You either have a job offer from a company, or the option of getting a residence permit, if we’re talking about the European Union.
Those who left later aren’t necessarily people who have it easier. In many ways, it can be the opposite: harder for them. For example, because of the work of ICE in the United States, migrants’ lives there have become much more unpredictable. Attitudes toward Russians are also changing in the European Union — Germany, for instance, effectively stopped issuing humanitarian visas in 2025, even to those who fear persecution from Russia.
Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin.
I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language daily news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine.
Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore.
None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them.
— Do people handle a second or third move more easily, or does each subsequent one wear them down even more?
— Among OutRush’s respondents from 2022–2024, many had already changed their country of residence, and some had even changed countries five or six times. How people handle moving, across the sample as a whole, depends on the person’s age and whether they’re burdened with family and children. But overall we quite rarely come across people who genuinely enjoyed it, though these people did exist too.
I remember an interview from Latin America: the person ended up there after making a huge journey through Asian countries. He deliberately chose not to go to the nearby European Union, because he didn’t want problems stemming from his Russian passport. And he was happy with his choice.
— If the situation in Russia keeps getting worse, but not too drastically, will people keep leaving, or will they get used to it at some point and the outflow will stop?
— Both processes happen at the same time. On one hand, people really do adapt to almost anything. What was perceived as an emergency four years ago is gradually becoming part of everyday life. So the same deterioration in conditions can provoke a much weaker reaction a few years later.
There’s also a self-selection effect. Many of those for whom it was easiest to leave — people with foreign languages, remote jobs, international connections, savings — have already done so. Increasingly, those who remain include people for whom the cost of emigrating is especially high: elderly parents, children, mortgages, a profession that’s hard to transfer to another country, lack of money. So a worsening situation doesn’t automatically translate into a proportional rise in emigration.
But adaptation also has a limit. Gradual deterioration often produces not a smooth curve of emigration but a series of steps: for a while almost nothing happens, then a trigger appears, and we see a spike. There’s another important point: the worse the economic situation gets, the more people may want to leave, but the fewer people can afford to. So rising discontent within the country doesn’t necessarily translate into an equivalent rise in actual emigration.
How Russian emigrants are adapting abroad (spoiler: not badly)
— What do your respondents call themselves? It seems like many, for example, don’t really like the word “emigrant.”
— In April 2027, a book I co-authored with two other researchers is coming out, bringing together the results of all our work over the past several years. One of the chapters, and the beginning of the book, is devoted precisely to how people refer to themselves. We spent a long time thinking about what to call them, because many people find the word “migrants” unpleasant, partly because it echoes migrants within Russia. We often characterize Russians who left after February 2022 as advanced, urbanized people who understand ideas about coloniality within Russia. But many still don’t like calling themselves migrants, because it seems to lower their social status.
Some people like the word “relocant,” because it reflects that you’re in demand, since someone is willing to relocate you. But according to our data, the share of these people is very small. Those whom employers actually hired and relocated, providing them with a package of services including hiring and housing, are an absolute minority. The very term “relocants” is misleading, because it attributes more privilege to the whole group than may actually exist. There’s even a kind of judgment built into the word: the implication that these are people who don’t need and don’t deserve empathy or support, because they can survive on their own.
The way we — researchers, journalists, or states — sort people shapes narratives. And these are dangerous because we build cause-and-effect chains from them, which then translate into specific countries’ political decisions. If Russians are “relocants,” then they’re not entitled to any help. And conversely, you also can’t call everyone refugees, because refugees are, first and foremost, Ukrainians. And then a kind of moral economy kicks in: whose suffering is more important and deserves more attention.
There are other self-designations too: many call themselves a “global citizen,” a “citizen of the world.” In English there’s the word exile and the phrase person in exile. These are the terms we actually use in the book.
— What themes and issues come up most often in the words of the migrants you’ve spoken with?
— In addition to the surveys, we collected 581 interviews with Russians who ended up in more than 60 countries. And at least back in 2023–2024, the country of residence didn’t have that much effect on how people talked about themselves. There was also a lot of dark humor: people often resort to memes and self-deprecation to describe their often difficult situation.
— How successfully are Russians adapting abroad?
— In the first two years of the [full-scale] war, according to our surveys, two-thirds of the people who left in 2022 and had previously worked for Russian companies (including remotely) left those jobs and were able to find new ones. But it’s worth remembering that a fairly large share of Russians who left work in the IT sector, where, at least until the AI boom, things were pretty good. People employed in science and teaching had it hardest of all: finding work abroad is very difficult for them.
— Do emigrants often integrate into local society, or do they more often end up strictly within their own community?
— Based on the material from our 2023 interviews, we can say that people don’t learn the host country’s language well. The first survey data showed that everyone was rushing to learn Georgian, Armenian, or whatever language [of the country] they’d moved to. But over time, most Russians have continued to stay within the Russian-speaking community, even if they think that’s the wrong thing to do.
Yet Russians are often accused of not forming diasporas, even though those who left after 2022 are actually successfully creating groups where they communicate with each other. This community is united by a shared moral shock and by being against the war. And earlier waves of emigration — in the 1990s, for instance — didn’t have that kind of unifying foundation. In this wave of migration we see almost no desire to distance oneself from one’s compatriots, and that’s a very significant shift.
— In one of your papers there’s a concept called discordant privilege, a phenomenon where a migrant’s identity seems to split in two. Can you tell us about this idea?
— This concept comes up in the article about Kyrgyzstan. The thing is, our respondents sometimes “jokingly” mentioned a ranking of countries where you could end up. The coolest ones were, say, Luxembourg, Switzerland, probably the United States. And at the very bottom was Kyrgyzstan. On one hand, you can see an element of disrespect and a colonial attitude toward less economically prosperous countries in this. On the other, this hierarchy reflects internal inequality among those who left themselves. Russia is one of the most unequal countries in the world, and it’s naive to assume that the people who left it are all the same. Not everyone is an IT worker with [a monthly salary of] $5,000. Kyrgyzstan often became the destination for people who, for example, couldn’t move to European Union countries because they lacked connections.
So, we had one interview in Kyrgyzstan where a person who had left Russia quickly found work in healthcare, because Russian-language medicine is in high demand there. He arrived with a sense of “I’m a colonizer, someone who should treat this former Soviet country carefully.” But to his surprise, he was treated with great respect. So discordant privilege is the mismatch between how you’re seen in the host country and how you assume you’ll be seen. You move from one hierarchy into another and have to reconcile your previous position with the positions of the host society.
— It sounds like you’re describing a kind of logic of deservingness and guilt — that you have to prove you hold the “right” antiwar views in order to be accepted in a country. Is that something Russian emigrants experience?
— Yes, many Russians who left retain a sense of guilt in Thomas Mann’s understanding of the term. If we ask respondents in a survey who bears responsibility for the war, most will say: we’re guilty, Russia is guilty. But interestingly, when we start unpacking that emotion in interviews (what exactly should you atone for, and to whom?), a lot of nuance emerges. A person can fully acknowledge that a crime is taking place while denying individual guilt. Many interviewees insist that the host country should judge them only by their individual actions, not by their Russian passport.
Do emigrants believe they’ll ever return home
— How has emigrants’ perception of the war changed over the past year compared to 2022?
— Data comes in very slowly, and I don’t have anything new for 2026. I can point to not-yet-published information from our study in Armenia (though, of course, that can’t give us a complete picture of all emigrants). Overall, attitudes toward the war haven’t changed. It remains a common view that Russia should bear responsibility for rebuilding Ukraine if there’s ever some kind of peace process.
Meanwhile, skepticism toward the West is growing. There’s a study, for example, of Russians in the United States and Poland that confirms disillusionment with democracy in the host countries. The processes underway, especially in America in connection with ICE’s work, are causing many to become disillusioned with European–American democracy. And in Europe we’re also seeing a powerful anti-migration turn. It’s not connected to Russians, but they too are getting swept up in that same vortex and are becoming victims of the rightward shift in European politics.
— It seems like among those who left for political reasons, there are more and more people experiencing apathy and, conversely, withdrawing from politics. How accurate is that?
— Yes, that’s absolutely true. A colleague and I recently published a paper looking at how people demobilize. Among our respondents were people who blossomed after emigrating and became more involved in volunteering: helping the homeless or organizing fundraisers. But more people who had actively participated in political initiatives became demobilized.
The first reason is emotional burnout. My colleagues published a detailed paper on this in 2025, with testimony from Russian emigrants. People burn out in a stream of bad news with no light at the end of it. They’re squeezed on one side by host countries, where they must constantly prove they’re not a security threat or simply maintain their legal status, and on the other by the need to keep thinking about possible threats from their own country. It’s a psychologically unhealthy situation.
The second reason is financial. Activists, media outlets, and human rights advocates lost their sources of support when the largest American donors and many other sponsors withdrew their backing. They’ve had to reinvent themselves in a new reality. The third reason is transnational repression. Many still have relatives and property, some continue traveling to Russia, and these serve as levers of pressure that hold people back.
The Russian diaspora isn’t unique in this respect. If you look at other studies — for example, on the diaspora of people who left Turkey, since Erdogan also triggered several waves of academics and activists leaving the country — you’ll see that the more time passes, the more people demobilize, because they need to see light at the end of the tunnel. If that light isn’t particularly visible yet, people start switching to something else.
But that doesn’t mean no one is engaged in politics anymore. A great many people who left Russia continue to take part in civic initiatives in one way or another, often shifting to less visible forms of activity for safety reasons.
— Compared to 2022, do emigrants more often describe their departure as final? Do many say they won’t return to Russia even if the situation improves significantly? You’ve written that if a person has stayed in emigration for more than two years, the likelihood of returning drops significantly.
— When people are asked why they left and whether they want to return, they can say anything, because they often orient themselves around “correct” and “incorrect” answers. How people will actually behave is a separate, open question. But it really is true: if we understand anything about migration — any migration, not just Russian — the longer people stay abroad, the higher the likelihood they’ll remain there. Two years is more of a rough benchmark. The process can be nonlinear. But it’s roughly the amount of time in which a person can establish themselves in a new place — for example, finding a job and permanent housing.
There are people who left for political reasons who continue to live in Russia in their heads, even though they’re technically not there. For example, offices of many political and civic organizations in exile are located in Vilnius and Berlin. I imagine many people there go to work “in Russia.” Someone out there is surely still living out of a suitcase. There were very few of these people in our interviews, but they existed. One person said: “I still haven’t unpacked my suitcase. If something happens tomorrow, I can just grab it and fly back.” I don’t know if he’s still hasn’t unpacked his suitcase.
— Are there many among your respondents who say they’ve found a genuine new home in emigration?
— That happens, but it’s rare. For most people, the dominant trope is that of the guest, a motif of gratitude and hospitality toward the host country: “We really appreciate that we’re tolerated here.” But the specific sense that this is my new home is rare. Rather, respondents have a sense that they’re gradually getting used to it, which sounds more like resignation.
But the good news is that Russians in emigration have managed to build many communities. And that, I think, is a major breakthrough. I remember when I first flew to the United States as a student in the early 2000s, I met a Soviet migrant who told me: “If you need help, never approach someone who speaks Russian. Better to ask an American for help.” His words, that level of distrust toward what were nominally his own people, really surprised me.
But after 2022, Russians in emigration, united by shared misfortune and shared trauma, displayed forms of civic behavior every bit as strong as those of citizens of any advanced democratic country. For example, they’ve created aid projects like Kovcheg, Emigration for Action, and Idite Lesom [“Get Lost,” an organization assisting Russian deserters]. They cooperate with activists in host countries and open bookstores selling Russian-language books, like Babel in Berlin. Places like these serve as gathering points for the community.
Therefore, when someone says there’s something wrong with our civil society, I want to respond: “We’re fine. The problem isn’t us, or at least, not only us.”

articles.title: Araghchi holds a series of talks in NY on regional security, Hormuz and Iran-EU ties
articles.body:
Araghchi holds a series of talks in NY on regional security, Hormuz and Iran-EU ties
TEHRAN– Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held a series of meetings with foreign counterparts on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, engaging Russian, British, Portuguese, Bruneian, Kyrgyz, Polish, Spanish, Egyptian, Jordanian, Cypriot, Pakistani and Austrian officials on regional security, the Strait of Hormuz, the war in West Asia, Palestine, Iran-Europe relations and bilateral cooperation.
Hormuz and Regional Security
The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the future of maritime navigation emerged as a recurring issue in Araghchi’s meetings with European and regional officials.
In talks with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Araghchi briefed his counterpart on Iran-Oman discussions concerning arrangements for a safe maritime route through the Strait of Hormuz. He also outlined diplomatic efforts by mediators to establish conditions for a return to negotiations.
In separate talks with Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel and Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger, Araghchi attributed the disruption of maritime traffic and insecurity in the Strait to US and Israeli military actions. He said, from Iran’s perspective, restoring maritime security would require an end to 'destabilizing US measures and economic pressure.'
Araghchi also raised regional security with Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, criticizing the use of the territory of regional states in military operations. He said Iran was prepared to work with neighboring countries on security arrangements based on regional cooperation rather than external military involvement.
The Iranian foreign minister’s discussions with Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev and Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski also touched on the wider regional crisis. With Sikorski, Araghchi warned against linking the Ukraine conflict to developments in West Asia, urging European governments to address security challenges on their own continent while taking positions on regional developments based on international law.
Iran-Europe relations
Relations with European governments formed another major thread of Araghchi’s meetings.
During talks with British Foreign Secretary Edward Miliband, Araghchi criticized Britain’s political and military support for Israel and called on London and other European governments to reconsider policies contributing to instability in West Asia.
The two sides also discussed Iran’s nuclear program. Araghchi reiterated Tehran’s stated preference for resolving outstanding issues through diplomacy and criticized Britain, France and Germany over their positions concerning the so-called snapback mechanism and the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran’s nuclear facilities.
Similar concerns were raised in Araghchi’s meetings with the foreign ministers of Spain and Cyprus. He called on European governments to base their policies toward Iran and the region on international law and avoid 'alignment with parties responsible for aggression.'
Palestine and wider regional conflict
The Palestinian issue was central to Araghchi’s discussions with Brunei’s Foreign Minister Abdul Mateen ibni Hassanal Bolkiah, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi.
Araghchi called for greater coordination among Islamic countries and a more active role for the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in addressing the situation in Gaza, the West Bank and Al-Quds. He also emphasized the need to support Palestinian self-determination and efforts toward establishing an independent Palestinian state.
With Abdelatty, Araghchi discussed strengthening bilateral coordination alongside regional developments, while his meeting with Safadi focused on regional security and cooperation between Iran and Jordan.
Russia, Pakistan and regional diplomacy
Araghchi and Lavrov also reviewed political, economic, trade, transportation and energy cooperation between Iran and Russia, as well as coordination within international organizations. Lavrov reiterated Moscow’s opposition to 'US and Israeli military aggression against Iran' and emphasized adherence to international law and the UN Charter.
In New York, Araghchi also held talks with Pakistani Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar on bilateral relations and regional developments. The meeting came as Pakistan was pursuing a mediating role between Iran and the United States.

articles.title: Iran offers seven-day peace plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz, but Trump is in no rush
articles.body:
Iran is pushing a fast-track agreement that it says could end the war, halt fighting in Lebanon and reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, before immediately launching negotiations over its nuclear program.
But U.S. President Donald Trump, who has said an agreement will come “eventually,” either before or after the November midterm elections, appears in no hurry to surrender the naval blockade that has become one of Washington’s most powerful sources of leverage over Tehran. Iran, meanwhile, is maintaining its own hard line.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday that Tehran would show no flexibility over its nuclear program and would reopen the Strait of Hormuz only after “all of its conditions are met.”
The official did not spell out those conditions, but Iranian officials have previously demanded an end to the U.S. naval blockade, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil sales, the release of at least $12 billion in frozen Iranian assets and an end to the war “on all fronts,” including Lebanon.
The comments came as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi remained in New York, where his spokesman said indirect contacts with Trump representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff could continue.
Araghchi held three hours of talks with Witkoff and Kushner on Tuesday, mediated by Qatar on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The New York Times reported that he was expected to remain in the city through Monday.
At a briefing for international reporters on Thursday, Araghchi outlined Iran’s latest proposal. According to reports, it is essentially an accelerated version of the memorandum of understanding reached in June, an agreement widely seen as giving Tehran significant gains, including a role in managing traffic through the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian officials told the Times that Tehran now wants to implement the agreement’s complicated series of steps far more quickly than the original 60-day timetable.
Araghchi said the entire process could be completed within a week, after which negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program would begin immediately.
But Tehran is demanding significant concessions first: an end to hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon; the release of frozen Iranian funds; the lifting of the blockade on Iranian ports; and sanctions relief allowing Iran to resume oil sales.
If those conditions are met, Araghchi said, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen “by the end of the seventh day.”
He added that it would be “better” to reach an agreement before the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Trump has an incentive, but also leverage
On paper, Trump has a powerful political incentive to secure a deal before the elections.
Even the announcement of an agreement could drive down oil and gasoline prices, which have surged since the war began and amid Iranian attacks on tankers using the Strait of Hormuz. Polls have shown deep frustration among U.S. voters over rising prices, an issue Republicans fear could hurt them in the battle for control of Congress.
Yet Trump has repeatedly said he is in no rush to strike a deal.
The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that Washington had informed Tehran, through Qatar, that Trump did not intend to lift the naval blockade, as he did following the June agreement before reinstating it in July.
A White House official told the Journal that the blockade, combined with tougher sanctions that this week severely disrupted Iran’s aviation sector, had put Washington in a “strong position” against Tehran.
“President Trump is open to talks with Iran under the right circumstances, but he has no need to negotiate with the Iranians,” the official said.
Trump also remains deeply suspicious after several previous understandings with Tehran unraveled soon after they were reached, whether because of disputes over implementation or divisions inside Iran’s ruling establishment.
Hard-line elements in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been accused of carrying out attacks on ships after previous understandings were reached.
That has also raised questions over how much authority Araghchi, regarded as a more moderate figure within the Iranian establishment, actually has to conclude an agreement. Hard-liners inside Iran have already criticized the renewed contacts with Washington.
Iranian official: Chances of diplomacy are ‘extremely low’
Ali Vaez, director of the Iran program at the International Crisis Group, told the New York Times that Tehran’s proposal was a “smart move.”
“They know this is very tempting for President Trump, because it ends an unpopular war and lowers energy prices ahead of the midterms,” he said.
At the same time, Vaez noted, the proposal would revive an agreement that was largely favorable to Iran, while the compressed timetable for reaching nuclear negotiations could appeal to a president eager for rapid results.
Iran has its own reasons to want an agreement before the U.S. elections.
Beyond Tehran’s urgent desire to lift the blockade and sanctions as its domestic economic crisis worsens, many analysts believe Trump could face fewer political constraints after the midterms and could become more willing to resume an intensive military campaign against Iran.
Trump himself threatened during his address to the UN General Assembly this week to “destroy” Iran if it failed to reach an agreement with him.
Reuters described both sides as confronting essentially the same dilemma: Washington and Tehran each want an agreement, but neither wants to surrender its main source of leverage without receiving something tangible in return.
For Trump, that leverage is the blockade. For Iran, it is the severe disruption of traffic through Hormuz. The United States maintains that the strait is not technically closed, although shipping remains drastically reduced.
If Washington and Tehran cannot turn that leverage into an agreement before the elections, the diplomatic window could narrow as the risk of escalation rises.
A senior Iranian official quoted in the same report warned that Tehran would respond forcefully to any American escalation.
“Our finger is on the trigger,” he said. “The Americans know what they need to do, but because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this crisis are extremely low.”
According to regional sources who spoke to Reuters, Tehran is prepared to drop its demand that ships pay transit fees to pass through Hormuz from the main agreement.
Iran, however, still wants the demand included in a separate annex. The sources said Tehran would regard any arrangement as temporary and would not formally abandon its claim to authority over the strait, which is an international waterway and was open to unrestricted commercial traffic before the war.
This time, Saudi Arabia is pushing against concessions
Another obstacle has emerged from the Gulf.
Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states are now opposing an agreement with Iran, at least one resembling the June memorandum of understanding, according to reports by the Associated Press and Wall Street Journal.
Saudi Arabia had supported renewed diplomatic efforts during the summer and opposed a return to war. Its position has now shifted.
People familiar with the discussions told the Journal that both Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were urging Washington not to make concessions to Tehran, including lifting the blockade on Iranian ports or easing economic pressure.
Another official told AP that the change was driven by the escalating confrontation with the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen.
The Houthis have attacked Saudi oil facilities and, during their latest territorial advances in Yemen, seized areas commanding the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the strategic passage linking Europe and Asia through the Red Sea and Suez Canal. Its importance has grown further as traffic through Hormuz has been severely disrupted.
The official said Saudi Arabia had previously been able to “live with” an agreement that granted Iran some degree of control over Hormuz.
That calculation changed, he said, after the Houthi advances and an attack by militias in Iraq on Saudi Arabia’s strategic East-West Pipeline, which allows the kingdom to export oil through the Red Sea while bypassing Hormuz.
The Wall Street Journal reported that a similar shift had taken place in the UAE, which previously supported diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.
Emirati officials are now playing down expectations for talks with Tehran following recent confrontations with Iran and continued attacks on vessels in Hormuz.
Gulf states, the Emirati officials were quoted as saying, should not accept a settlement that gives Iran permanent control over the strait.
Meanwhile, sources described as knowledgeable told Iran’s Fars news agency on Friday that reports of a new round of negotiations and the dispatch of Iranian experts to New York were false.
“The reports about new talks are intended to influence the market and oil prices,” they said.

articles.title: Defense official: Russia's neighbors have stepped up responses to air threats
articles.body:
Defense official: Russia's neighbors have stepped up responses to air threats
Due to Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine, more and more drones and even cruise missiles have ended up in neighboring countries, which is why the Baltic states and Poland have strengthened measures for responding to air threats, said Gert Kaju, head of the Ministry of Defense's defense readiness department.
The side effects of Russia's aggression are increasingly being felt in countries adjacent to the war zone; for example, 39 drones have entered Moldovan airspace this year, Kaju said on Friday at the weekly briefing held at the Ministry of Defense.
"In addition, drones have been shot down in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and also Romania. And Russian cruise missiles have also ended up in third countries — they have either flown through that airspace or somehow veered into it," he described.
"In response to this, the procedure for deploying air‑defense assets has been made faster, primarily in Poland and also in the direction of the Baltic states — meaning the chain of command has been simplified and accelerated in order to respond to this air threat," Kaju said.
According to the overview presented by the Ministry of Defense representative, Russia continues long‑range strikes on Ukraine's critical infrastructure, hitting residential buildings, industrial enterprises, administrative buildings and transport infrastructure in at least 14 oblasts over the past week.
"According to Ukrainian data, Russia has launched circa 1,900 jet‑powered drones in September, of which Ukraine claims to have destroyed circa 60 percent," he noted. "Due to these attacks, Ukraine has lost nearly 90 percent of its steel‑production capacity."
Ukrainian strikes against energy infrastructure
With its long‑range strikes, Ukraine hit oil‑refining plants in various Russian regions during the previous week of the war, including in Moscow, Yaroslavl and Samara oblasts. As a result of the strikes, Russia's oil‑refining capacity has suffered additional losses; Russia is losing production capacity, Kaju said.
"In addition to infrastructure related to oil refining, Ukraine continues to strike Russia's logistics centers, including in the Moscow region," Kaju added. "As for medium‑range strikes, here Ukraine's drone units have focused primarily on airfields in Crimea and Rostov oblast, as well as areas related to drone storage and launch sites, and also additional energy facilities in Crimea."
According to Kahju, more than 400 different energy facilities in Crimea have been hit since early July, and in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea Ukraine has managed to put more than 300 vessels out of action.
Fighting continues in Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv oblasts
Speaking about what is happening on the front line, Kaju said that the most intense fighting is still taking place in Donetsk oblast, in the direction of Pokrovsk and Kostyantynivka, as well as in the direction of Lyman. Following these in intensity are Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv oblast.
Ukraine has carried out counterattacks primarily in Kharkiv oblast, including in the direction of Kupiansk, and in Donetsk oblast, where Ukraine's focus is primarily on the Lyman direction.
"Russia's combat losses are 1,500 soldiers per day, and therefore we can say that Russia's weekly losses are over ten thousand soldiers," Kaju stated.
Russia's threats and propaganda continue
Kaju also spoke about how Russia continues rhetoric in which it blames everyone else for what is happening in Ukraine, including Ukraine and the Western world, with Moscow claiming that the Western world is using this situation to generally escalate relations with Russia.
"Russia also continues pressuring countries that support Ukraine, so that they would abandon supporting Ukraine," he said. "As an example, we can point out the situation where the Russian Foreign Ministry summoned the chargé d'affaires of the United Kingdom in Moscow and issued an official protest against London's further increase of arms deliveries to Ukraine. At the political and communicative level, Russia continues to spread its worn‑out narrative," Kaju described.
"In addition to the fighting and the air threat described above in neighboring countries, hybrid activity has increasingly come into view in third countries — whether direct acts of sabotage, various types of information operations or other such activity. That is, companies involved in supporting Ukraine are threatened, attempts are made to attack them or force them to stop their activities," the Ministry of Defense official said.
"All of this is part of Russia's narrative, where their goal is to create fear and uncertainty on the other side, because creating fear and uncertainty is one part of Russia's deterrence policy, trying through this to show that Russia is a large and threatening force," he explained.
"Our response to this must be, on the one hand, that we monitor it, respond to these steps with our own steps, and in the case of incidents it is also important to attribute the event to its initiator," Kaju emphasized.
"So in summary — one thing is the war in Ukraine, but on the other hand its effects are increasingly felt in neighboring countries, primarily through the hybrid activities described above. Our task is to monitor and respond to them according to the nature of the threat," Kaju said.
--
Editor: Mait Ots, Argo Ideon

articles.title: Saudi Arabia kept nuclear weapons option open, according to US intelligence assessment: US media
articles.body:
Muhammed Yasin Güngör
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Months after Saudia Arabia and the US signed a bilateral civil nuclear pact, classified intelligence assessments recently provided to the US Congress conclude that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons program, The Washington Post reported Friday.
US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that the evaluation forms part of intelligence documents submitted to lawmakers alongside material from the US State Department, which expressed greater confidence in Riyadh's commitments and the agreement's oversight safeguards.
"With this deal, the Trump administration is departing from precedent, adopting looser restrictions, and caving to Saudi demands by agreeing to a process that is all but certain to allow Riyadh to acquire the means to enrich uranium and possibly develop nuclear weapons," a coalition of Democratic lawmakers, led by US Senators Ed Markey and Jeff Merkley, wrote Friday to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a former Republican senator.
The US State Department defended the arrangement, maintaining in a statement to the Post that Washington "does not and will not support a Saudi nuclear weapon program."
Abdulaziz bin Salman, the Saudi energy minister, said earlier that the civilian effort remains "peaceful" and operates under "the highest levels of responsibility and transparency."
Under the bilateral civil nuclear pact signed this July by Abdulaziz and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Washington agreed to supply technology and fuel while granting a conditional pathway to domestic enrichment, limiting levels below 5% before potentially authorizing up to 20% following additional review.
The agreement sits under a 90-session-day congressional review timeline following its August submission, facing a Joint Resolution of Disapproval introduced by House Democrats over non-proliferation concerns.

articles.title: Iran still not seeking to obtain nuclear weapons — president
articles.body:
NEW YORK, September 25. /TASS/. Iran still has no intention of obtaining a nuclear weapon, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Fox News in an interview.
When asked whether his country had any desire to acquire a nuclear warhead, he said: "Absolutely no."
"Our martyred revered Supreme Leader [Ali Khamenei] said several times in the past that this is religiously forbidden. From the religious standpoint, it is prohibited to have a weapon of mass destruction," he added.
He reaffirmed his country’s readiness to observe the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).
"We have never sought to obtain a nuclear weapon. We want to comply with the Non-Proliferation Treaty," the Iranian president said.
In his words, Iran is ready for agreements with the United States, and is putting forward demands only within the framework of the international law.

articles.title: AI, Cryptocurrency, and Shell Companies: How A7 Procures Components for Russian Defense Industry
articles.body:
Russian financial company A7 has developed an extensive network of shell companies that allows Russia to circumvent Western sanctions and procure goods for its defense industry.
The New York Times reported this, citing leaked internal company documents and an analysis of its software.
A7 was established in 2024 by Moldovan-Israeli oligarch Ilan Shor together with the sanctioned Russian Promsvyazbank PJSC. According to Western intelligence agencies, Shor oversees these activities under the direct command of the Russian presidential administration.
Kyrgyzstan served as the main financial hub for A7’s schemes for a long time. More than $100 million in U.S. dollars and Chinese yuan flowed through the bank accounts of local shell companies.
To evade international scrutiny, A7 developed a dedicated AI-powered system that automatically forged invoices and customs documents. Instead of dual-use electronics, the documents listed civilian goods such as car mats or light boxes.
In the first four months of 2025 alone, the company processed more than $500 million in prohibited transactions. More than $130 million of that went toward procuring products for Russia’s defense industry.
Among the purchased goods was steelmaking equipment from China’s Xi’an Heavy Equipment, which is used in the production of shells and armor. Payments were also made for Nvidia servers for AI development and video components for Walksnail drones.
A7 obtained foreign currency for international transactions by transferring Gazprom’s revenues from gas sales in the UAE. The funds were converted into U.S. dollars, euros, and the Tether stablecoin.
Overall, the company claims to handle one-fifth of Russia’s annual foreign trade turnover, amounting to approximately $130 billion.
After Kyrgyz authorities closed the accounts of several shell companies under Western pressure, A7 quickly shifted its operations to other jurisdictions. Journalists identified at least 71 affiliated companies in the UAE, Bahrain, Nigeria, Qatar, and Mongolia.
Despite the imposition of sanctions on Shor and affiliated entities, the scheme remains highly flexible and continues to operate through the constant creation of new legal entities.
It is worth noting that Chinese state-owned company Jilin Chemical Fiber Group supplied raw materials to Russia’s defense industry for the production of strike drones.

articles.title: Iran hands US plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz within seven days
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran hands US plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz within seven days
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday that Tehran had offered Washington a plan that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened to maritime navigation within seven days once agreed.
Araghchi met for talks on Tuesday with Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the US-Israeli war and reopening the vital energy shipping channel.
"Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi said at the UN Friday.
"The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure.
"I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared."
Earlier media reports suggest the new plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon.
It also reportedly calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least $12 billion, as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade of Iran.
On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz.
A US official told Reuters that positive, constructive discussions were ongoing through mediators when asked about the proposed seven-day plan.
Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of Iran's military, told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran's demands.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, reopen the strait and launch talks on Iran's nuclear programme.
But the deal broke down shortly afterward when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.
Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.
Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.

articles.title: Ukraine’s soldiers cracked problem US chased for 30 years: a drone that ferries combat robot deep into enemy rear
articles.body:
Ukrainian soldiers have built a drone that carries a combat ground robot into battle and drops it where needed, a trick the US has pursued but never fielded. The Alter Ego battalion of the 93rd Mechanized Brigade has paired a bomber drone with a purpose-built robot, the Desantnyk, and took it from idea to combat in 10 days, the Brave1 defense cluster said.
The system answers a problem that has long hobbled ground robots: getting them to the fight over mined, cratered terrain they cannot cross on their own.
A drone carries the robot dozens of kilometers behind the lines and drops it precisely, in a pairing engineers call a "marsupial", one carrier delivering another. The US worked on such systems for more than 30 years, Brave1 said.
And it is not alone: the 3rd Army Corps has been air-dropping robots behind Russian lines in its Vivaldi offensive.
A drone carries the robot in
The Desantnyk is a compact wheeled platform. Alter Ego built a way to release it accurately from a heavy bomber drone, dropping it well beyond the range a ground robot could reach on its own. It lands deep in the enemy rear and drives on to its target. The point is to spare the robot the most dangerous, exposed leg of the journey.
Confirmed kills follow fast
According to Brave1, just 10 days passed from the idea to its first combat use, and the Desantnyk has already carried out confirmed strikes: the unit used it to destroy Russian shelters and troops. Only a handful of Ukrainian units have mastered the tactic so far.
Brave1 moves it to production
The defense cluster, a state platform for scaling battlefield inventions, said it took notice of the Desantnyk and helped the battalion find a manufacturer to move it from prototypes to serial production and out to other units.

articles.title: Seventeen makers head to Michigan to test bomber drones for the Pentagon, and Ukrainian firms are back in field, some under US partners
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone makers are getting another shot at a Pentagon contract, this time for bomber drones. Seventeen companies, including Ukrainian firms and Western partners fielding Ukrainian designs, will test bomber drones at Camp Grayling in Michigan in October, the next stage of the Pentagon's Drone Dominance program, Defender Media reported.
The Phase 2.5 Bomber Qualifier is the latest round of the Pentagon's drive to buy combat-tested drones at scale, and Ukrainian makers are again in the field, some through US-registered partners, because Pentagon rules bar direct sales from foreign firms.
This time, the target is bombers, the drones that drop munitions on what is below them.
Seventeen makers head to Michigan
The contest runs at Camp Grayling, a Michigan training range, and organizers call it the hardest and fastest-paced stage of the program yet. Each company must bring at least six fully built systems.
The testing splits into two parts: a Bomber Qualifier, which the makers conduct themselves, and a Bomber Gauntlet run by US soldiers. Organizers have not published details of a third mission. Winners of the wider program earn Pentagon supply contracts.
Ukrainian bombers make the list
The invited firms include UFORCE USA Services, Grim Tech, Gurzuf Defence, UA Defense Tech, Skycutter, and UDD Tech Corp. Which models they will bring is not yet clear.
UFORCE is known for its Nemesis bombers. Grim Tech showed a light bomber, the Grim-18, at the MSPO defense expo in Poland this month, and Gurzuf builds heavy bombers, including the Ayudag-6, which recently set a Ukrainian payload record for multirotor drones at 130 kilograms.
A second try after a US sweep
In the program's last phase, the Pentagon picked five winners in each of two categories, and all were American, though a Ukrainian firm had reached the second round and, by industry accounts, Ukrainian designs were incorporated into some Western entries. For Ukraine's makers, the bomber round is another chance to turn battlefield-proven hardware into a US contract.

articles.title: UK kept Israel arms flowing despite Gaza evidence: report
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK ignored Gaza legal warnings to keep Israel arms flowing: report
Internal UK government documents reveal that ministers continued to approve arms exports to Israel despite receiving assessments warning that its conduct in Gaza could breach international humanitarian law, according to a new investigation.
Hundreds of pages of Foreign Office assessments obtained by Channel 4's Dispatches show how the British government examined alleged Israeli attacks on civilians, aid workers and humanitarian sites as it considered whether Israel was complying with international law.
The documents informed decisions on whether Britain could legally continue licensing arms exports to Israel during its war on Gaza.
The investigation found that officials examined hundreds of graphic videos and reports documenting civilian deaths, but the government concluded in the overwhelming majority of cases that there was insufficient information to determine that Israel had breached international humanitarian law, because Israel itself had not provided "sufficient evidence" on incidents examined.
Ramita Navai, the reporter and a producer on the investigation, told The New Arab: "Something has gone deeply wrong with the way both the Conservative and Labour governments have dealt with allegations of and evidence for Israeli war crimes."
"The apparent bias towards Israel means our government may have breached international law," she said, adding, "Our institutions should never be bent for any ally, and there needs to be accountability, especially when it is about genocide."
Legal experts interviewed by Dispatches questioned the methodology behind the assessments, saying the process made it extremely difficult to reach a finding against Israel when the Israeli military did not provide sufficient information about its targets or military objectives.
Professor William Schabas, an expert in international human rights and criminal law who reviewed the assessments, said the methodology appeared to be structured in a way that produced findings that violations had not taken place.
"My impression from looking at all this material is that the British government has adopted what looks like a methodology, but one designed to produce a result that no violations are taking place," he told the programme.
Israel has previously accused Schabas of bias against it, an allegation he rejects.
Cameron received warnings over humanitarian aid
The documents also shed new light on what former Foreign Secretary David Cameron knew about concerns over Israel's conduct.
In January 2024, Cameron was repeatedly questioned by parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee over whether he had received legal advice suggesting Israel was violating international humanitarian law.
He declined to give a direct answer, saying he could not recall every document he had received.
But Dispatches says Cameron had received two assessments only weeks earlier concluding that Israel's restrictions on humanitarian relief could potentially breach international humanitarian law.
An email obtained by the programme recorded that Cameron had "carefully considered all the information" contained in one assessment.
Despite the warnings, Cameron determined that Israel remained committed to complying with international humanitarian law overall and arms exports continued.
The investigation also reveals that Cameron later concluded Israel had not been committed to complying with international humanitarian law regarding humanitarian relief during a period between December 2023 and January 2024.
However, he said that finding did not require existing arms licences to be suspended.
In a letter obtained by Dispatches, Cameron also noted that suspending licences would have a "significant impact on UK interests".
Civilian deaths deemed 'inconclusive'
Among the incidents examined by officials was an Israeli strike on a compound in Al-Mawasi housing four British doctors working with Medical Aid for Palestinians and the International Rescue Committee.
The compound was located inside an Israeli-designated humanitarian zone and its location had been coordinated with the Israeli military.
Despite receiving what Dispatches described as inconsistent explanations from Israeli officials, the government's assessment concluded there was insufficient information to determine whether the strike represented a possible breach of international law.
Other cases included an attack on Al-Fakhoura school in Jabalia refugee camp, where at least 24 Palestinians were reported killed, and the killing of five-year-old Hind Rajab, an incident that gained widespread public notoriety as being emblematic of Israel's conduct in Gaza.
Rajab was trapped in a car with members of her family and pleaded for help by telephone before she was later found dead.
The assessments did not reach conclusions on whether international law had been breached in those cases because officials said they lacked sufficient information from Israel about the military objectives involved.
The Israeli military initially denied that its forces were present in the area in the immediate aftermath of Hind Rajab's killing, and later admitted in August 2026 that its soldiers had fired on the car.
The programme also examines the Israeli strike on a World Central Kitchen convoy in April 2024 that killed seven aid workers, including three British veterans.
Israel acknowledged responsibility for the attack, calling it a "grave mistake", and dismissed two officers.
Two days after the attack, while Cameron was publicly demanding answers from Israel, his office approved a decision not to suspend existing arms export licences, according to the investigation.
Officials warned 'system is broken'
The investigation also details concerns within the Foreign Office over Britain's handling of the war.
Several senior officials told Dispatches that tensions between civil servants and ministers over Gaza were deeper than during any previous conflict.
They said officials had been instructed not to use terms including "ethnic cleansing" and "genocide" in reports, while hundreds of civil servants raised concerns about the risk of British complicity in alleged war crimes.
Former diplomat Mark Smith, who had previously worked on assessments of British arms sales during the Saudi-led war in Yemen, resigned from the Foreign Office in August 2024 over the government's refusal to halt arms sales to Israel.
"The nature of the assessment is such that you can kind of make it say whatever you want. And that is why the system is broken," Smith told Dispatches.
UK assessment examined genocide allegations
A June 2024 government assessment obtained by the programme also stated that it was "uncontentious" that the physical components of genocide were present in Gaza, while concluding that genocidal intent on Israel's part had not been established.
The UK government's position under both Conservative and Labour governments has been that determinations of genocide should be made by competent courts following full judicial processes.
Israel rejects allegations that it is committing genocide in Gaza or deliberately targeting women and children.
After Labour came to power in July 2024, Foreign Secretary David Lammy suspended around 30 arms export licences to Israel after the government found a "clear risk" that some British-supplied equipment could be used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law.
The suspension did not cover British-made components entering the international supply chain for F-35 fighter jets.
A spokesperson for Lammy rejected suggestions made by the programme concerning the timing of legal advice he received, saying the relevant advice was dated nearly six weeks before his decision to suspend licences and that "many events unfolded" during that period.
The Foreign Office defended its procedures, saying Britain's processes for assessing international humanitarian law risks and arms exports were "among the most robust and rigorous in the world".
"Officials provide impartial, evidence-based advice and ministers take decisions on that basis. Any suggestion that assessments were not conducted professionally and rigorously is wrong," it said.
The Israeli military claims it operates "solely based on military necessity and in strict accordance with international law" and reportedly takes precautionary measures to reduce harm to civilians.
Chris Doyle, Director of the Council for Arab-British Understanding, told The New Arab that the investigation is "just continued evidence that previous governments ignored, deliberately or through negligence, all the evidence that Israel was systematically violating international law in Gaza."
Doyle said that the position of the UK government towards Israel's conduct in Gaza contrasted with its position in other conflicts, including in Syria and Ukraine, and he welcomed the recent changes brought about by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
"Israel has to be held accountable for its actions, but also those in the United Kingdom and elsewhere who facilitated or enabled this also have to answer for what they have done or not done," he added.

articles.title: Ukraine is trading access to 5 million frames of real combat for British AI technology: they use the data inside locked platform
articles.body:
Ukraine is opening its battlefield data to British weapons makers so they can train their AI on a war no one else has fought. Up to 12 British defense companies will join Avengers Labs, Ukraine's platform for training AI models for drones and robots on real combat data, the Defense Ministry said.
Ukraine's combat data is a resource no other military has access to. British firms get to build and test their AI on battlefield data they could not access elsewhere, while Ukraine gets their technology and joint development of AI for unmanned systems.
What is Avengers Labs?
More than 30 Ukrainian companies already use the Avengers Labs, and three of their systems have reached the battlefield. It is part of the AI push former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov built around Ukraine's data.
The terms are built around control. The British companies can develop and test their own AI models within Avengers Labs, the ministry said, but the data remains within the platform's protected environment, with no way to download it or take it out. That lets Ukraine share the value of its war experience, the annotated record of real combat, without surrendering the record itself.
The platform was developed by the Center for Innovation and Development of Defense Technologies, the team that created the DELTA combat system. At the core of Avengers Labs is an annotated dataset of 5 million frames collected on the battlefield. Most of this material comes directly from the DELTA combat system and is continually supplemented with new data of practical value in combat conditions.
Britain trains for a real war
In March 2026, Ukraine announced the establishment of a system of military technology competence centers. The first in the network was intended to be the Defense AI Center "A1," which would focus on AI solutions.
The AI center is being launched with support from the UK. Its main tasks were planned to be:
analysis of combat data;
forecasting enemy actions;
development of autonomous systems;
new management/control tools
A separate center was said to have been established for each key direction of the war: drones, mid-range strike, deep strike, artillery, and others.

articles.title: Russian drones struck a McDonald's warehouse - Zelenskyy showed the latest aftermath in Kyiv
articles.body:
Russian drones struck a McDonald's warehouse - Zelenskyy showed the latest aftermath in Kyiv
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked a McDonald’s warehouse in Kyiv with a drone. Four people were killed and seven injured, including a child, as a result of the strike on the office building.
Russia struck a warehouse used by "McDonald's" with drones during its ongoing attack on Ukraine. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported this on social media on September 25, showing the aftermath of the enemy strike in Kyiv, UNN writes.
What is known about the consequences of Russia's attack in Kyiv as of now
"As of this time, four people are known to have been killed as a result of Russia's drone strike on an office building in Kyiv. My condolences to the families and loved ones. Seven more people were injured, including a child. I thank all our emergency services, which always promptly help people after Russian attacks," Zelenskyy wrote.
Russia's strike on McDonald's warehouse
There were also drone strikes today on a warehouse used by McDonald's. An attack drone against ordinary products. The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centers, internet providers—everything that constitutes ordinary life is simply a target for Russia. All of this undermines people's ability to stay connected, study, and work
The President emphasized: "It is important that the world's response to all this exists and that Russia feels the consequences of its terror. Our long-range capabilities and the world's sanctions must work together precisely toward this—to create concrete consequences for Russia."

articles.title: The SBU detained an FSB agent who was preparing an attack on a UAV manufacturing facility
articles.body:
The SBU detained an FSB agent who was preparing an attack on a UAV manufacturing facility
Kyiv • UNN
A resident of Lviv region transmitted the coordinates of a drone manufacturing facility to the FSB in preparation for a missile strike. He faces life imprisonment.
The SBU military counterintelligence exposed an FSB spotter. He turned out to be a resident of Lviv region recruited by the enemy, who worked at a facility producing unmanned systems for the Defense Forces in western Ukraine. This was reported by the press center of the Security Service of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
According to the investigation, the suspect was supposed to guide a Russian missile strike against this facility in order to disrupt the uninterrupted supply of strike and reconnaissance UAVs to Ukrainian defenders.
To carry out the intelligence assignment, the suspect tried to "leak" to the FSB the geolocations of the administrative, production and storage premises of the potential "target." The enemy also hoped to obtain from the "mole" information about when the largest number of people would be present at the restricted-access facility. SBU officers exposed the enemy’s plan in advance and detained the agent
During searches conducted after the detention, investigators found and seized a tablet from the suspect, which he had covertly used to receive and transmit intelligence, as well as to communicate with his FSB handler. The investigation established that he had been recruited by the Russian special service through a Telegram channel offering "easy" earnings.
The detainee was notified that he was suspected under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law). The perpetrator faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.
To remind you
The Security Service of Ukraine detained two suspects in the explosion near a Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center in Mykolaiv, Stryi district, Lviv region.

articles.title: Iran Uses Chinese Satellite Data to Attack U.S. Bases – CNN
articles.body:
Chinese satellites are providing Iran with intelligence data and imagery, which has significantly increased the accuracy of Iranian attacks on U.S. military facilities and civilian vessels in the Middle East.
This was reported by CNN, citing U.S. intelligence assessments and sources within the U.S. government.
According to intelligence reports, it was Chinese intelligence that enabled Iran to launch a precision strike on a U.S. base in Jordan in July, killing three U.S. service members.
In addition, Chinese satellite data helps Iranian forces track the movement of ships in the Strait of Hormuz and effectively deploy drones during large-scale attacks.
U.S. officials note that, in addition to Chinese support, the accuracy of Iranian weapons has improved thanks to Russian assistance and accumulated combat experience.
It is worth recalling that Russian reconnaissance satellites may also have provided Iran with data for precision strikes on U.S. targets in the Middle East, including an air base in Saudi Arabia.
Two days before the Iranian attack, 14 Russian reconnaissance satellites, including the Kosmos-2573, flew over the Prince Sultan Air Base near Riyadh.
