articles.title: If the drone orders are not paid for in October–November, there will be problems in winter — Zelenskyy
articles.body:
If the drone orders are not paid for in October–November, there will be problems in winter — Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine must pay for orders of drones and missiles in October–November to ensure deliveries at the beginning of the year. The EU and the IMF support efforts to find the funds.
Ukraine must finance orders for drones in October–November to ensure their availability for January–February. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated this, reports UNN.
Details
As for the 27 billion. Certainly, this includes, in part, funding for our soldiers, but mainly it is money for our drones, missiles, and support for our soldiers. But what is important is that about a third of this money, or perhaps even slightly more, is for drones for January, February, and March. If we do not order and pay for them in October and November, we will face serious challenges in January and February
He added that Ukraine had discussed this in detail with the European Union, the President of the European Commission, and the International Monetary Fund.
We discussed what programs could be put in place and how to help Ukraine. The International Monetary Fund has nothing to do with military support or drones; there are completely different issues involved, while I am strongly asking the European Commission to bring forward the second tranche from the 90 billion, because, once again, January and February must be supplied with the relevant drones and missiles
He also noted that the EU and the IMF had responded positively and constructively.
Everyone understands that it is very important to cover this deficit. Everyone understands that Ukraine cannot be left alone, that more must be invested in Ukrainian-made drones and missiles, because most of this deficit consists precisely of funds for this—for weapons. Everyone understands how difficult it is to get through this period and the constant strikes, but nevertheless, Ukraine will not—once again, will not—be left alone. The EU supports us, and the IMF will continue its programs—here I received a positive response from our partners
Going forward, according to Zelenskyy, the Prime Minister of Ukraine, together with the Minister of Finance and the Head of the Foreign Intelligence Service, must work out all the details concerning coverage of the deficit. According to him, some of these funds may be raised in the format of a Drone Deal.
The Ukrainian team is working on the details, and a meeting with the European team in Ukraine or Belgium is planned in the near future
We remind you
The European Commission is examining the possibility of accelerating the provision to Ukraine of €45 billion earmarked for 2027 as part of the EU’s €90 billion loan program.

articles.title: Trump asked Ukraine’s Zelensky to meet Putin in the Russian capital for peace talks
articles.body:
Trump asked Ukraine’s Zelensky to meet Putin in the Russian capital for peace talks
- President Trump urged Ukrainian President Zelensky to meet Russian President Putin in Moscow for peace talks, but Zelensky declined and expressed frustration.
- The US is pushing for a truce on attacks against energy assets amid rising global diesel prices, but neither Ukraine nor Russia has agreed.
- Trump supports banning US diesel exports to curb prices before elections, raising concerns in Europe about fuel shortages and inflation.
AI generated
NEW YORK – President Donald Trump this week again encouraged Volodymyr Zelensky to travel to Moscow to meet with Vladimir Putin, despite repeated past refusals, as the US looks to reignite Ukraine-Russia peace talks.
Zelensky declined the appeal made in his meeting with the US leader at the United Nations, and people familiar with the Ukrainian president’s position said Trump raising the issue upset him.
When asked by reporters when he would visit Moscow, Zelensky replied: “On a missile,” followed by an expletive.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Zelensky and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov each held separate meetings with Trump administration officials in New York this week. The US has pushed both sides to agree to a truce on attacking each other’s energy assets as global diesel prices surge, but neither has accepted.
Zelensky said on Sept 25 that technical peace negotiations with Ukraine and Russia will likely take place in the United Arab Emirates, though the US has not yet proposed a date.
European officials say Trump and his team were receptive to their lobbying efforts on support for Ukraine before winter sets in. They also said Trump’s meeting with Zelensky was largely positive.
Trump has not decided whether he will send Ukraine more air defence supplies this winter, as the US grapples with its own shortages due to the Iran war, but has agreed to grant Ukraine licences to produce Patriot missiles.
Zelensky said on Sept 25 that Trump told him he’d made the final decision this week, though did not elaborate on the timing of deliveries. Production is not expected to start for at least a year, so will not address Ukraine’s more urgent need to protect its critical infrastructure assets against Russian attack over the colder months.
Trump’s suggestion of a Russia meeting came the same week Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the US has invited Putin to attend the Group of 20 summit in Florida in December, a statement met with criticism in Europe.
The European Union’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas told CNN that the announcement “was very hard to hear.”
People close to the Kremlin have suggested that Putin is likely to skip the G-20 anyway and attend a summit hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping in November.
Europe is also growing worried about a push by some Republican lawmakers to ban US diesel exports. Trump this week said he supports the idea, with wars in Iran and Ukraine driving the fuel’s price to record levels.
A pause in exports would force Europe and Latin America to search for hard-to-find alternatives, adding to inflationary pressures around the globe. Trump is under pressure to address the high cost of diesel in the US before the November midterm elections. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Iran says it awaits US response on seven-day roadmap to end war
articles.body:
Iran says it awaits US response on seven-day roadmap to end war
Tehran says the plan would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks within a week if Washington agrees.
Iran has formally submitted a seven-day roadmap to end its war with the United States and is now awaiting Washington’s response, according to Tehran’s top diplomat.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi detailed the plan to reporters outside the United Nations Security Council on Friday, saying it had been conveyed to Washington through Qatar.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iraqi airports halt Iranian flights after new US aviation sanctions
- list 2 of 3UAE bars Iranian airlines as US sanctions squeeze Iran’s aviation sector
- list 3 of 3What’s in Iran’s seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz?
“The seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” he said.
Araghchi noted that initial steps would take four to five days, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen on the sixth day and “on day seven, the talks with the US will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects”, referring to Iran’s nuclear programme.
The offer and its conditions
Under the plan, Washington would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, release an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and observe a ceasefire covering the region, including Lebanon and Yemen.
In return, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas passed before the war, and which has become Tehran’s main point of leverage.
“The choice now rests with the United States,” Araghchi said.
“Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. I can tell you if there is seriousness on the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared.”
Ending all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Yemen and Lebanon, was reportedly among Tehran’s demands.
A plan that echoes a collapsed deal
The proposal, which aims to end the war that has entered its seventh month, closely mirrors a memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed between Tehran and Washington on June 17, after Qatari and Pakistani mediation, which set a 60-day window for talks but collapsed within weeks.
Technical and vague terms over control of shipping through Hormuz led to disputes, as Iran began firing on vessels it accused of ignoring its authorisation rules, prompting US President Donald Trump to declare the deal “over” in July.
The US has since sporadically struck Iranian territory and coastal areas in response.
Araghchi met for talks on Tuesday with Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. Witkoff said the meeting was “lengthy” and that he hoped the talks would “prove constructive and promising.”
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Fox News this week that ending the war was now up to Washington. “It’s America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not,” he said.
A White House official told CNN the Trump administration was having “positive and constructive discussions through the mediators”.
Analysts, however, remain sceptical.
“Basically nothing has really changed,” said Cyrus Schayegh of the Geneva Graduate Institute, arguing Iran wants to keep the leverage it gained during the war, while Washington resists returning to the June framework.
It appears unlikely that the new deal will make major progress before the US midterm elections in November, though Araghchi said Friday it “would be better” to reach one beforehand.
Qatar, a key mediator in the conflict, said its foreign minister spoke with Pezeshkian on Friday about de-escalation and the conditions for renewed dialogue.

articles.title: Newest AIM-9X Missiles Not Meeting Operational Availability Goal
articles.body:
One of the Air Force and Navy’s most common air-to-air missiles is falling short of a key readiness metric, and the services are ramping up stocks of a vital air-to-ground missile, according to recent Pentagon reports.
The Modernized Selected Acquisition Reports on the AIM-9 and the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, cleared for publication in July, lay out progress and shortfalls and provide a snapshot for the health of these key munitions.
According to the reports, the AIM-9X Sidewinder Block II is facing operational availability shortages. The Warfighting Acquisition University defines operational availability as “the degree … to which one can expect a piece of equipment or weapon system to work properly when it is required.” The Air Force is at 58 percent operational availability for the latest version of the Sidewinder, and the Navy is at 78 percent—the requirement is 86 percent, the report says.
That shortage is forcing squadrons to face lower training asset availability, preventing fighter pilots from having the requisite number of Captive Air Training Missiles. Those CATMs have live seekers and guidance units that pilots use on regular training sorties to practice locking onto targets, tracking high off-boresight angles, and simulating missile shots.
When enough training pods are nonoperational, aircrews don’t have enough rounds to fly daily air-to-air tactical training with realistic seekers.
The Air Force and Navy plan to buy more than 11,000 AIM-9X Block II missiles, which are infrared-guided, short-range, supersonic air-to-air weapons.
But reliability problems with integrating a new circuit processor into the latest configuration, the AIM-9X-4, have “impacted missile reliability and halted testing.”
As a result, a software update called Operational Flight Software 10.4, meant to integrate the advanced guidance control unit and inertial measurement unit hardware upgrades, will not be fielded.
Report authors note that the follow-on software that will fix the problem won’t be ready until September 2027.
AIM-9X maker RTX declined to comment on the report.
JASSM and LRASM Work
As the two services work out the air-to-air missile problem, both are seeking to expand their plans for the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles and its cousin, the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile.
Another shared munition between USAF and the Navy, the JASSM is a linchpin munition with multiple variants fielded and in production.
The AGM-158A JASSM is a 14-foot-long missile that strikes beyond 200 miles and has been a staple of U.S. aircraft use since 2001. The B-1B Lancer, B-2A Spirit, B-52H Stratofortress, F-15 variants, F-16 variants, and C-130 Hercules can carry it and its variants, and the F-35A Lightning II and B-21 Raider are planned to integrate it.
The AGM-158B JASSM-Extended Range can hit targets at more than twice the distance, with public reports showing ranges of more than 500 miles.
The AGM-158C LRASM has a range closer to the baseline JASSM but is equipped with radio-frequency seekers designed to strike large, moving targets such as ships.
According to the recent selected acquisition report, the joint program office between the two services had delivered 5,348 JASSM variants to the Pentagon as of April, according to the report.
Current production capacity sits at about 600 JASSMs annually, with near-term plans to reach 860 missiles a year.
More mid-term plans call for ramping up that production to 1,280 missiles annually by fiscal year 2030 and 1,880 by fiscal 2032, according to the report.
A March $52 million contract modification to LRASM will raise the missile’s production from 240 per year to 320 per year beginning in fiscal 2029, according to the report.
Lockheed announced a new JAASM option at AFA’s Air, Space, & Cyber conference earlier this month, the AGM-158 FLEX.
The company sees FLEX, a modular, designed munition which has swappable nose and launch options, as another way to offer a variety of strike options in the JASSM form factor.
“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.
The stockpile plus-up, however, will use current factory space via expansion efforts, the Eglin spokesperson wrote, and “will not require a new facility construction.”
Lockheed’s investment strategy includes $8 to $9 million through 2030 to meet heightened munitions demand.
“We are expanding production and building and modernizing more than 20 facilities in Arkansas, Alabama, Florida, Massachusetts, and Texas,” Lockheed spokesman Scott Swofford told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email. “This includes upgrading existing facilities and incorporating advanced manufacturing techniques, production lines, tooling, and plant layouts to meet urgent production demand.”
Software, Paint, and Engines
Like the AIM-9X, the JASSM also faced software integration problems, specifically with its 54.0.02 flight software update. But an Eglin spokesperson said the software had received fielding approval since data for the selected acquisition report was gathered in April, and that “there are no impacts to combat readiness.”
The Air Force is also pressing to accelerate the integration of the Universal Armament Interface, a software architecture to standardize aircraft mission systems-weapons interface, but this has introduced “added software risk,” according to the report.
But the Eglin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the UAI program has “made no changes to the delivery schedule” of the JASSMs.
“Integration activities remain on track to deliver planned capabilities as scheduled. Software risk is being actively managed through early software-in-the-loop integration, resource prioritization, and agile contract actions,” the spokesperson said.
Separately, the report noted that in an inspection of 1,356 JASSMs, inspectors flagged 49 missiles for depot-level maintenance and overhaul, mostly due to stealth coating defects. The report says that issue won’t be resolved until 2029.
Lockheed switched from the flat gray paint scheme to a semi-gloss black coating to reduce radar and visual signatures. The new coating can absorb and deflect electromagnetic energy more easily during longer flight times used by the new, extended-range variants.
The shift began in 2021 with the Lot 19 contract award for the AGM-158B-2 variant.
The Eglin spokesperson said that both the program office and Lockheed Martin are “exploring contracting actions to increase repair capacity and return serviceable missiles to the field more efficiently.”
Beyond software updates, the Air Force also spent $200 million in fiscal 2025 to procure and mature a second-source engine for the LRASM and JASSM-ERs.
“Investing in a second engine source for the AGM-158 is essential to securing our supply chain and ramping up production of critical long-range strike weapons,” the Eglin spokesperson said. “By establishing a second production line, we eliminate manufacturing bottlenecks, drive competition, and secure deliveries of JASSM and LRASM to the warfighter.”

articles.title: Zelenskyy warns $27B funding gap could leave Ukraine short of weapons
articles.body:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky (R) and High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas (L) attend a joint press-conference following talks in Kyiv on October 13, 2025. | Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images
KYIV — Ukraine needs to secure $27 billion to plug a hole in its defense budget in the next two months or risk being unable to buy weapons early next year, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters in a WhatsApp chat Friday.
“Most of this money is for our drones, missiles, and supplies for our warriors. About a third of this money, perhaps even a little more, is for drones for January, February, and March. And if we do not order and pay for them in October and November, we will face serious challenges in January and February,” Zelenskyy said.
The president added that covering the deficit was a top topic of his negotiations with European partners: “I am urging the European Commission to provide the second tranche of the €90 billion [loan] sooner. Because, once again, we must have the necessary drones and missiles for January and February.”
Advertisement
Ukraine first announced the budget gap in August. It emerged after Ukraine had to bring forward state defense spending originally planned for the second half of the year, as Hungary delayed the EU’s €90 billion loan to Kyiv. Purchases made included "fiber-optic drones, middle-strike drones, interceptors,” former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov told POLITICO in June.
The shortfall remains despite €30 billion in funding Europe has already pledged to Ukraine this year as part of the €90 billion loan.
Zelenskyy said he received a positive and constructive response from the EU during his diplomatic talks this week.
“Everyone understands that covering this deficit is very important. Everyone understands that Ukraine cannot be left on its own and that more must be invested in Ukrainian-made drones and missiles, because most of this deficit is precisely the funding needed for that,” Zelenskyy said.
EU member countries on Friday agreed on the terms for releasing €6.6 billion in European Peace Facility funds for Ukraine, the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said in a statement.
"€900 million are for the EU’s Military Assistance Mission for Ukraine. €1 billion will fund new joint procurement of equipment. And €4.7 billion will reimburse Member States, with some already saying they will channel their share to Ukraine," Kallas said.

articles.title: Putin claims Ukraine attacked polling stations in Russia
articles.body:
Putin claims Ukraine attacked polling stations in Russia
Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin has claimed that Ukraine carried out strikes on polling stations in Moscow on the night of 19-20 September.
Source: Kremlin-aligned Russian news agency TASS, broadcasting Putin's press conference on 25 September
Details: Putin claimed that Ukraine had disrupted all negotiations that had been taking place in Istanbul, but had announced its readiness to resume the talks ahead of Russia's elections.
Quote: "Indeed, we said that negotiations would hardly be possible before the State Duma [lower chamber of the Russian parliament – ed.] elections, but after that we would be ready to resume these engagements. But what has happened recently is also well known: on the night of 19-20 September – on the main voting day – there was an attempted large-scale attack on Moscow.
More than 1,600 drones entered the Moscow zone. Polling stations were hit."
Details: Putin complained that a school housing a polling station had supposedly been hit and was "practically destroyed". The Russian leader also claimed that the homes of polling station heads had come under attack.
He said all proposals for a peaceful settlement are "on the table", but Russia still needs to consider what is in its interests.
Putin also stressed that Kyiv has no way to counter Geran drones and said Kyiv should "feel the response" through attacks on "civilian infrastructure".
Background:
- On the night of 19-20 September, Ukraine launched a large-scale drone attack on Moscow and Moscow Oblast. A major fire broke out at the Sofyino logistics technopark. The Moscow Oil Refinery in the Kapotnya district also caught fire following the attack.
- Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin called it the largest-scale drone attack on the Russian capital.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the defence forces used a number of Ukrainian long-range weapons during the overnight attack on Moscow Oblast, including Flamingo, Palianytsia and Pelican.
- The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported that three units at the Moscow Oil Refinery had been damaged in the strike.

articles.title: Russia not preparing for war with Europe – Putin
articles.body:
Russia not preparing for war with Europe – Putin
Moscow is not preparing for military action against European countries, President Vladimir Putin has said, dismissing claims of a Russian threat as an attempt to inflame tensions.
Speaking to the media on the sidelines of the 12th United Cultures Forum in St. Petersburg on Friday, Putin said European countries were fueling tensions in order to continue supporting Ukraine.
He accused “aggressive circles” in Europe of seeking to use Ukraine as “cannon fodder” to constrain Russia’s development.
Putin described remarks by the Estonian Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur about a possible conflict with Russia as a “provocation,” and referred to statements about the benefits of a preemptive attack on Russia as “political clownery.”
“The circus has left, but the clowns remain,” he said.
Putin also addressed the prospect of renewed talks with Kiev, saying Moscow would base any decision on Russia’s own interests.
According to the president, Ukraine has been actively raising the prospect of a ceasefire, including on attacks against energy infrastructure, as well as an end to the blockade of Russia’s Black Sea coast, while continuing its own strikes on Russia.
Russia responded to attacks on civilian, Putin said, particularly pointing to the “mass” Ukrainian attack on Moscow on September 20, as well as attacks on residential buildings and election officials. He described Russia’s retaliation as “sensitive and destructive” for Ukrainian forces.
“They must feel these retaliatory strikes by Russia and understand that no provocative actions, no escalation of the situation will lead to the result they want. They will only make their position worse,” the Russian president said.
According to Putin, claims that Moscow intends to attack Europe are being used to justify continued spending on Ukraine to European citizens. 
“This is complete nonsense,” he said.

articles.title: What US doesn't tell about its army
articles.body:
It is still far too early to fully grasp the scope of the costs and consequences of the US war waged against Iran. A conflict that Washington’s initial calculations envisioned as short-lived has dragged on for months, keeping a significant portion of US military capabilities tied down in the region for an extended period. What we know about this war today is largely derived from official statements, media reports, remarks by US officials, and scattered documents—a picture in which significant aspects appear to remain hidden.
The latest example is the aircraft carrier *Abraham Lincoln*. According to an ABC News report, the Acting Secretary of the US Navy confirmed in a letter to Congress that a total of eight suicide attempts have been recorded among the personnel of this strike group since the *Lincoln* began its deployment. These figures are not limited to the ship's own crew but also encompass personnel from the air wing, the strike group staff, accompanying destroyers, and the aviation squadrons deployed aboard the vessel.
Of course, US Navy officials have stated that this figure does not necessarily fall outside the typical pattern for a long deployment and that they treat every case seriously. Yet, that is precisely the crux of the matter: the *Lincoln* is not merely an aircraft carrier; it could serve as a case study of the pressures the US military has endured during this conflict.
The ship was scheduled for a routine six-month mission in the Pacific, but the war with Iran altered its course, resulting in an unusually long deployment. The *Lincoln* ultimately remained at sea for 286 days—spending more than 200 of them in the operational zone, according to published reports—and the families of some service members spoke about the strain caused by this extended deployment.
Even the Acting Secretary of the US Navy acknowledged in August that the war disrupts routine schedules and that extended missions and combat operations place immense strain on the forces. At the time, he cited figures including 266 days of deployment, 200 days spent in a combat zone, over 10,000 flight sorties, and the expenditure of approximately 1.5 million pounds of munitions.
However, alongside this official narrative, other details have gradually emerged. Reports concerning the *Lincoln* have highlighted the restriction of contact between troops and their families during critical periods, changes to meal plans when resupply was difficult, technical issues, and the strain caused by a prolonged deployment. US officials have acknowledged some of these issues, contrasting with the different account of the carrier's situation that had been presented previously.
To that, the *Lincoln* must be viewed as more than just a story about eight suicide attempts. The significance of this vessel lies in the fact that it has been one of the largest and most iconic instruments of US military power during a protracted war. If an aircraft carrier—with its thousands of military personnel—has faced such a combination of pressures and issues after nearly 300 days of deployment, the more critical question is: what has been the situation for other US forces at the bases, on the ships, and in the units involved in this war?
There is an important fact: information regarding the actual performance of the US military in a conflict is typically released with a time lag. Some information remains classified for security reasons, while other details may only come to light months later through congressional documents, audit reports, military investigations, troop testimonies, or media coverage. The US Navy itself maintains a vast volume of operational documents and ship-related reports—compiled as operational records and logs—to which public access is not immediate.
Thus, what we know about the *Lincoln* today likely resembles a single piece of a larger puzzle rather than the complete picture. Eight suicide attempts do not, in themselves, prove the collapse or failure of the US military; yet, when viewed alongside 286 days of deployment, over 200 days in a combat zone, operational strain, limited contact with family, and issues that U.S. officials have been compelled to acknowledge, a serious question arises: what aspects of the US military's actual condition in this war remain undisclosed to the public?
It may take months or even years for a more complete picture of the true cost of this war for the US military to emerge. Only then will it become clear whether what we know today about the *Lincoln* was an isolated case or a sign of broader problems about which there is not yet sufficient information.
In such circumstances, one should not look solely at statistics regarding casualties and destroyed equipment. War is not limited to what is visible on maps or in footage of attacks; the attrition of forces, the prolongation of missions, psychological strain, supply chain disruptions, diminished readiness, and the costs of maintaining a military force during a protracted conflict are also part of the reality on the ground.
The *Lincoln* holds special significance in this regard, as it served as a symbol of US military might during the conflict. Now, after a deployment spanning nearly 300 days, the vessel itself has revealed information indicating that a more complex reality lies behind the imposing imagery of aircraft carriers and the projection of American military power.
And perhaps this is the most important point: what has been published so far regarding the state of the US military in this war is not necessarily the end of the story; it may well be just the beginning of the revelation of costs—aspects of which have not yet been fully disclosed to the public.
MNA

articles.title: US not to include Patriot system missiles in $400 million aid package for Kiev — Reuters
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, September 26. /TASS/. The United States will not include interceptor missiles for the Patriot air defense systems in a $400 million military aid package for Ukraine, Reuters quoted sources as saying.
According to the report, the administration of President Donald Trump has committed to spending the $400 million allocated for military aid to Ukraine before the end of the current fiscal year, which ends in the country on September 30.
The story says this military aid is to be sent to Kiev by October 2029 and will consist of weapons, including parts for armored vehicles. A source said that "the military equipment did not include Patriot missiles" requested by Ukraine.
In July, the agency reported that the Washington administration notified Congress of its intention to complete the transfer of $400 million in military aid approved by lawmakers to Kiev no earlier than between the beginning of October 2028 and the end of September 2029. Senator Dick Durbin (Democrat, Illinois) previously said that the White House is refusing to transfer the $400 million to Kiev, even though it was approved by Congress.

articles.title: 'Lithuanian skies are NATO skies': DW interview with Lithuania's prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius
articles.body:
Lithuanian prime minister urges stronger NATO air defense
September 25, 2026
Lithuania is on NATO's eastern flank, bordering Belarus and Russia's Kaliningrad region. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, security has become one of the country's central political priorities.
The 42-year-old Mindaugas Sinkevicius recently took over as prime minister and also leads Lithuania's Social Democratic Party, a moderate center-left political force. In an exclusive interview with DW, he said he is concerned by the growing popularity of populist and far-right parties across Europe, particularly in Western Europe. But he also argued that the picture is more complicated, pointing to Social Democratic governments in several European countries and signs of renewed support for the center-left elsewhere.
For Lithuania, the war in Ukraine is closely connected to its own security. The country has experienced a series of incidents involving drones, instrumentalized migration and weather balloons entering its territory from Belarus. Sinkevicius said these developments have contributed to a broader sense of insecurity across Europe.
"As politicians, we have to tell society the truth," he said, identifying air defense as Lithuania's most urgent security priority.
"Lithuania's airspace is NATO's common airspace. Lithuanian skies are NATO skies," he said. "If Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO's skies are largely protected as well."
Drone incidents in Lithuania and beyond
Sinkevicius said Lithuania is seeking greater solidarity from its allies, pointing out that the threat goes beyond its national borders. A series of incidents involving drones have affected other European countries as well.
Sinkevicius stressed that NATO membership does not mean Lithuania can simply rely on its allies. Collective defense, he argued, works only when individual members are prepared to contribute.
"Of course, there is Article 5. Of course, there is collective defense," he said, referring to the NATO pact. "But at the same time, we need to do certain things ourselves, rather than relying solely on our partners, neighbors and alliances."
For Lithuania, this means strengthening its own deterrence capabilities while continuing to work through NATO and regional partnerships. He also pointed to the Nordic-Baltic Eight, or NB8, as an important framework for cooperation between the countries of Northern Europe and the Baltic states.
National security climbs national agenda
Sinkevicius rejected the idea that European countries should choose between traditional military equipment and newer technologies such as drones.
"Sometimes we see these issues being pitted against each other: drones versus tanks," he said. "I say we need both."
But for the Lithuanian prime minister, military equipment only goes so far. "Neither drones nor tanks will protect us if society does not feel safe, if people do not feel a connection with the state," he said.
For Sinkevicius, that connection is linked to social policy as well as defense. He argued that a state must also support people who are unemployed, ill or otherwise vulnerable.
The argument reflects a broader challenge for Sinkevicius as leader of Lithuania's Social Democratic Party. Traditionally, Social Democrats have focused more on social policy, education and healthcare than on defense. Russia's war against Ukraine has changed the political environment, forcing center-left governments in Europe to place national security much higher on their agendas.
Sinkevicius said the challenge is to increase defense capabilities without abandoning the principles of social democracy.
'We will continue to support Ukraine'
Sinkevicius recently traveled to Kyiv and Lutsk, some 400 kilometers (250 miles) west of the capital, where he met with Ukrainian political leaders. Lithuania has committed to allocating at least 0.25% of its GDP annually to support Ukraine. According to figures cited by the Ukrainian side, Lithuania's support in recent years has amounted to around 0.3% of GDP.
The prime minister acknowledges that some degree of war fatigue exists in Europe. But he said European societies should consider the scale of what Ukrainians have experienced.
"I sometimes ask myself: if we Europeans feel tired, then what must Ukrainian society be feeling?" he said.
Sinkevicius also pointed to the key role of Western European countries, particularly Germany, in maintaining support for Ukraine.
"Support and assistance must continue," he said. "Because if the Western front, figuratively speaking, weakens and falters, then on the eastern front — where Russia is fighting Ukraine — the risk of failure increases."
Edited by: Jess Smee

articles.title: U.S. Air Force Begins Independent Operations of FQ-44A Fury Unmanned Fighter
articles.body:
The U.S. Air Force has begun conducting independent flights of Anduril’s FQ-44A Fury unmanned fighter jet following the delivery of the first aircraft to the military.
This was reported by Anduril Industries on its official X account.
According to the company, the first Fury CCA was delivered to the U.S. Air Force in August. U.S. military personnel are now flying the aircraft without direct control from Anduril staff.
The Fury was transferred to an experimental unit at Krich Air Base, where military personnel are practicing its use alongside manned aircraft.
Following the transfer of the aircraft, the military began conducting several flights per day with it, while the presence of the company’s specialists at the base was significantly reduced.
In July, the FQ-44A had already undergone testing at Krich Air Base as part of the Agile Combat Employment concept. At that time, a single U.S. Air Force operator was able to launch and recover the drone independently after just a few hours of training.
During these tests, the Fury also flew alongside F-35 fighter jets. However, the F-35 did not directly control the drone—the aircraft operated under the control of its own Mission Autonomy system.
In addition, over the summer, the Fury conducted tests of the full air-to-air engagement sequence: it received an external target designation, processed it through the autonomous Lattice system, and fired an AIM-120 AMRAAM missile.
In September, the U.S. Air Force officially designated the aircraft as the FQ-44 Fury. The second CCA model in the program’s first phase—the FQ-42 from General Atomics—was named Vengeance.
Both aircraft are being developed as part of the Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program and are designed to operate alongside manned fighter jets, extending their range, situational awareness, and combat capabilities. The U.S. Air Force plans to have approximately 500 such aircraft by 2032, and eventually, about 1,000.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that Anduril had already begun serial production of the FQ-44A at its new Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio. The first production aircraft rolled off the assembly line in the summer of 2026.
The FQ-44A has already undergone testing with aerial bombs and other air-to-surface weapons, indicating plans to expand its role beyond aerial combat.

articles.title: Evan Gershkovich Says His Arrest in Russia Was Carefully Planned FSB Sting
articles.body:
U.S. reporter Evan Gershkovich, in his first detailed published account of his arrest in Russia in 2023, says he was the victim of an elaborate sting operation by the FSB security service.
In an extract from his book "This Cursed Beautiful Land," Gershkovich says that while working on a story for The Wall Street Journal about Russian military production, he held two meetings with the union boss of a factory in Yekaterinburg, a major defense-industry hub.
At their second encounter, in a steakhouse, the source produced papers with hand-copied tables of figures, telling the reporter that they related to the production of tanks.
As he jotted down notes, Gershkovich said, he heard the sound of marching feet and looked up to see a group of masked men approaching their table.
"A pang of guilt ripped through me: Had I compromised a source? But panic immediately replaced that thought. Instinct took over, my hands moving to hide the papers in the gap between the bench and the wall," he wrote in the book extract, published by the Journal on Friday.
"The men quickly descended on us. An arm was yanking my neck, pulling me off the couch... Someone shouted: 'You are under arrest by the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation'."
A long sentence, then a prisoner swap
Gershkovich, then 31, became the first U.S. reporter arrested on espionage charges in Russia since the Cold War. He was later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024.
He writes that he and his editors had considered the risks of the reporting trip and agreed that the source should not bring any documents to the meeting; if he did so, Gershkovich should not accept anything from him.
But at the meeting, the source had "thrust the papers into my hands."
Although he had reported on the arrests of other Americans in Russia, and on the targeting and even murder of Russian journalists, Gershkovich writes that the "unspoken rule" was that foreign correspondents enjoyed a degree of immunity: they might be expelled, but not arrested.
Reeling with shock, he was handcuffed, had a black sack placed over his head and was whisked into a van where he was placed in a chokehold and punched in the abdomen while being questioned, he writes.
FSB 'backup plan'
Gershkovich said that since his release he had learned of evidence that the FSB had a "backup plan" to arrest him on another of his planned reporting trips, to Siberia, if the Yekaterinburg operation had failed.
He said he believes the two meetings with the source in Yekaterinburg were designed to help the FSB persuade President Vladimir Putin that he was a spy and secure approval for his arrest at the second meeting.
"Putin, it seems to me, fully bought into this narrative," he said.
The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Putin said in a February 2024 interview with U.S. television host Tucker Carlson that Gershkovich had been "caught red-handed" while collecting confidential information.
The journalist, his newspaper and the U.S. government all strongly deny the allegation that Gershkovich was a spy.

articles.title: Pezeshkian uses UNGA meetings to press for diplomacy, and regional stability
articles.body:
Pezeshkian uses UNGA meetings to press for diplomacy, and regional stability
TEHRAN– Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian held a series of meetings with senior foreign officials on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, engaging the leaders of Pakistan, Lebanon, the Netherlands, Armenia and Bangladesh, as well as the presidents of Switzerland and the European Council, on regional security, diplomacy, bilateral relations and the consequences of the recent conflict involving Iran.
Pezeshkian also met with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Swiss President Guy Parmelin and European Council President Antonio Costa.
Across the meetings, the Iranian president placed particular emphasis on diplomacy as the means of resolving disputes, while arguing that pressure, unilateral measures and military force cannot provide a durable basis for regional security.
Diplomacy and search for a way out of regional tensions
The meeting with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre focused on the continuing instability in West Asia and the need to prevent further escalation. Pezeshkian called for international efforts to reduce tensions and create conditions for the restoration of regional security, stressing that disputes should be addressed through dialogue, international law and respect for national sovereignty.
Støre expressed concern about continuing instability, and particularly the potential international consequences of insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz. He also voiced support for diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions.
A similar emphasis emerged from Pezeshkian’s meeting with Swiss President Guy Parmelin. The Iranian president said recent US and Israeli military actions against Iran, including attacks on infrastructure and civilian facilities, were contrary to international law and humanitarian principles.
He nevertheless stressed Tehran’s readiness to develop relations with other countries based on mutual respect, sovereign equality and shared interests.
Parmelin highlighted Switzerland’s experience in diplomatic initiatives and its role as a protecting power for US interests in Iran, expressing his country’s readiness to maintain diplomatic contacts. The two sides agreed on the importance of political and diplomatic mechanisms to prevent another escalation.
Dialogue with Europe
Pezeshkian’s meetings with European officials also addressed the future of relations between Iran and Europe.
In his meeting with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, the Iranian president said Tehran remained open to dialogue but maintained that the United States must honor its commitments if diplomacy is to make meaningful progress. He argued that previous rounds of negotiations had repeatedly been followed by developments that disrupted the diplomatic process and ultimately contributed to war.
Jetten stressed the need for practical mechanisms to overcome existing obstacles in bilateral relations and identified maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz as one of the issues requiring diplomatic attention.
Pezeshkian took a more critical line in his meeting with European Council President Antonio Costa, arguing that European governments had diminished their ability to influence international developments by aligning themselves with US policies toward Iran.
He specifically criticized European positions on the snapback mechanism and the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), saying Tehran expected Europe to pursue a more independent approach.
On regional security, Pezeshkian argued that security should ultimately be ensured by the countries of the region, rather than through external intervention.
Relations with neighbors and regional partners
The Iranian president’s meeting with Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif centered on bilateral cooperation and regional diplomacy. The two leaders reviewed the implementation of existing agreements and discussed developments affecting regional security, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Peninsula.
Pezeshkian praised Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts to support regional peace and stability and called for continued consultations to prevent conflicts from widening. Sharif, for his part, reaffirmed Islamabad’s readiness to play a constructive role in regional diplomacy and highlighted the importance of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
With Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, Pezeshkian discussed Lebanon’s sovereignty and stability as well as the consequences of Israeli attacks. He reaffirmed Iran’s support for an independent and stable Lebanon and said Tehran favored regional cooperation and dialogue while respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states.
Salam outlined Beirut’s priorities, including an end to the Israeli occupation of Lebanese territory, the cessation of attacks and the strengthening of the Lebanese state’s authority.
Pezeshkian also met Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, with the two sides focusing on accelerating the implementation of bilateral agreements, particularly those concerning regional transit routes. Both leaders stressed the importance of translating existing understandings into practical cooperation.
Expanding economic and bilateral cooperation
Economic diplomacy was another component of Pezeshkian’s meetings. In talks with Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, the two sides discussed expanding economic relations and agreed on the importance of convening the sixth Iran-Bangladesh Joint Economic Commission.
Pezeshkian described the relationship with Bangladesh as possessing considerable potential for broader cooperation, while Rahman praised Iran’s assistance to Bangladeshi nationals during the recent crisis.
The meeting also addressed the wider regional situation. Pezeshkian reiterated that Iran would not yield to pressure but would continue engaging internationally on the basis of mutual respect and constructive relations.
A consistent diplomatic message
Taken together, Pezeshkian’s meetings in New York presented a consistent diplomatic message: Iran is seeking engagement with neighboring states, European governments and other international partners while opposing 'coercion, unilateralism and military pressure.'
The meetings also highlighted Tehran’s effort to connect regional security with diplomacy, arguing that lasting stability requires respect for national sovereignty, dialogue and regional mechanisms rather than externally imposed security arrangements.
At the same time, Pezeshkian used his encounters with European officials to press for a reassessment of Europe’s position toward Iran, particularly over the nuclear issue and its relationship with Washington, while meetings with neighboring and regional states focused more heavily on practical cooperation, transit, bilateral agreements and mechanisms for containing regional tensions.
The breadth of the meetings — spanning Europe, South and West Asia and the Caucasus — underscored the Iranian president’s effort at the UN gathering to keep diplomatic channels open while advancing Tehran’s positions on the regional conflict and the future of its international relations.

articles.title: Colombia cuts diplomatic ties with Iran under ‘influence of US and Zionist regime’
articles.body:
Colombia cuts diplomatic ties with Iran under ‘influence of US and Zionist regime’
TEHRAN — In a move that underscores a dramatic retreat from independent diplomacy toward subservience to the US regional agenda, Colombia’s newly inaugurated right-wing administration has unilaterally severed diplomatic ties with Iran.
The decision, enacted by President Abelardo de la Espriella on September 19, marks a sharp departure from the balanced, multipolar foreign policy pursued under former President Gustavo Petro. While Bogota has framed the move under the guise of “hemispheric national security,” diplomatic observers view the measure as a choreographed political concession aimed at currying favor with the United States and demonstrating alignment with its policies.
In an effort to rationalize its decision, the Colombian Foreign Ministry released a statement accusing Iran of maintaining connections with “narco-terrorist groups that threaten the security of the country.”
Yet, as with similar anti-Iran rhetoric recycled in Washington and Tel Aviv, Bogota failed to present a shred of credible evidence, intelligence briefing, or verifiable data to substantiate its sweeping accusations.
Tehran fires back: ‘Hypocritical deflection’
Reacting swiftly to Bogota’s hostile posturing, the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued an official statement on Friday, categorically rejecting Colombia’s unfounded allegations and condemning the abrupt rupture of bilateral diplomatic relations that span more than half a century.
The ministry stated in a statement that Bogota’s baseless accusations and simultaneous severance of diplomatic ties violate the foundational principle of mutual respect and run counter to the interests of both nations.
“It is evident that none of the claims put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical,” the statement emphasized, noting that the decision was adopted “solely under the direct influence of the United States and the Zionist regime.”
Turning the spotlight onto Bogota’s own deep-seated domestic crisis, the statement underscored that Colombia—which, by undeniable evidence, remains heavily influenced by illicit drug production and distribution cartels and effectively operates as part of the transnational narco-terrorism network across the Americas and beyond—is in no moral or legal position to lecture other sovereign states on terrorism and narcotics.
The ministry further stressed that such “hypocritical deflection cannot absolve the Colombian government of its international responsibility” regarding its complicity in the trafficking of massive narcotics shipments worldwide, including to Iran.
Highlighting a recent high-profile case, the ministry revealed that Iranian law enforcement seized a 55-kilogram shipment of pure Colombian cocaine in Tehran in September, which had been directly trafficked into the country by a network linked to influential Colombian figures. It described the seizure as one of the latest exposed cases of transnational organized crime attributed to Colombian networks.
The statement noted that rather than resorting to a hasty and hostile diplomatic rupture, relevant Colombian authorities were expected, under their international legal obligations, to cooperate with Iran in identifying the primary elements involved in trafficking this illicit consignment and similar shipments to Iran and the wider region.
The ministry concluded by warning that Iran reserves the right to take necessary measures in defense of its national interests in response to Bogota’s unjustified and hostile stance.
Strategic absurdity and logical fallacies
Tehran’s firm response highlights what political analysts describe as glaring logical fallacies and strategic absurdity behind Bogota’s claims.
First, there is the deeply flawed narrative regarding counter-narcotics. The insinuation that Iran—a nation that sits on the frontline of global counter-narcotics efforts and has sacrificed thousands of security personnel in combating transnational drug cartels originating from South Asia—would align itself with Latin American drug syndicates defies strategic logic. Tehran’s comprehensive counter-narcotics record is routinely acknowledged by international organizations, including the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC). Bogota’s attempt to project its own decades-long struggle with organized crime onto an external actor thousands of kilometers away is widely seen as an expedient deflection.
Second, regarding the instrumentalization of “hemispheric security,” this phrase is historically synonymous with the Monroe Doctrine—a framework long used to justify external interference in the sovereign affairs of Latin American nations. By invoking this outdated paradigm without tangible proof, the De la Espriella government is simply parroting long-debunked talking points crafted by hawkish think-tanks in Washington to justify isolating independent nations in the Global South.
Bogota further sought to legitimize its unilateral rupture by dragging extra-regional geopolitical disputes into bilateral affairs, lambasting Tehran for allegedly “blocking maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz” and “attacking countries in the Middle East.”
This claim completely reverses cause and effect, ignoring basic realities in West Asian waters.
As a guarantor of maritime security, Iran has historically served as the primary anchor of peace, stability, and navigation security in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian naval forces have consistently safeguarded commercial shipping lanes against piracy and unauthorized foreign military incursions. Accusations of “blocking traffic” deliberately ignore that any security measures enforced by Iran are fully grounded in international maritime law, innocent passage regulations, and the sovereign right to defend its territorial waters against unilateral foreign provocations.
Furthermore, regarding legitimate deterrence versus foreign hegemony, framing Iran’s defensive posture as aggression fundamentally misrepresents the regional dynamic. The root cause of regional instability in West Asia is not Iran’s defensive capabilities, but the destabilizing military footprint of the United States and Israel’s unchecked aggression. Iran’s military actions—carried out in full accordance with Article 51 of the United Nations Charter regarding the inherent right of legitimate self-defense—have been calculated, targeted responses to illegal strikes on its diplomatic premises, territorial sovereignty, and national interests. Equating Iran’s defensive deterrence with unprovoked aggression reveals Bogota’s uncritical adoption of Western talking points.
While the Colombian government noted it will maintain consular channels with Tehran, the abrupt severing of full diplomatic ties reflects an administration eager to dismantle sovereign South–South cooperation in exchange for short-term political alignment with external patrons.

articles.title: Russian elections expert Alexander Kynev stayed in the country to keep studying its politics. After criticizing the latest vote, he was arrested on drug charges.
articles.body:
Russian elections expert Alexander Kynev stayed in the country to keep studying its politics. After criticizing the latest vote, he was arrested on drug charges.
On September 25, several days after the State Duma elections, Moscow’s Perovsky District Court ordered political scientist Alexander Kynev detained on drug charges. Kynev, who had criticized the Kremlin over election fraud and administrative pressure during voting, was the country’s best-known expert on Russian regional politics. Meduza examines why he may have fallen afoul of the Russian authorities.
Alexander Kynev was born in the Komi Republic in 1975. By his own account, he left the Komsomol and became involved in the “democratic movement” in Ukhta when he was just 15. He didn’t say what that involved. But in his book “Kto i kak upravlyayet regionami Rossii” (“Who Governs Russia’s Regions and How”), he described the region’s political climate as the Soviet Union collapsed, including the first relatively competitive elections to local councils.
Kynev began working with the Yabloko party in 1996, first as an undergraduate and then as a graduate student in political science at Moscow State University. He worked with its regional branches and helped assess their work. By the 1999 State Duma elections, the 24-year-old was the chief expert on regional affairs at Yabloko’s central campaign headquarters. The party cleared the 5% threshold that year and won seats in parliament through its party list.
At Yabloko, Kynev worked closely with the team of politician and political scientist Vyacheslav Igrunov, one of the party’s founders, who oversaw its election campaigns. In 2001, Igrunov announced he was leaving Yabloko over a split within the party. Kynev formally cut ties with Yabloko the same day.
Kynev went on to work on various election and research projects. In 2002, he joined SLON, a social liberal party whose name stood for the Union of People for Education and Science. Igrunov formed it with allies from Yabloko and regional opposition politicians. SLON failed to win seats in the 2003 State Duma elections and ceased to exist five years later.
In the mid-2000s, Kynev worked as an analyst and researcher with many prominent organizations that studied Russian politics or monitored elections. He headed the analysis department at Golos, an independent election monitoring movement. At the Carnegie Moscow Center, which operated in Russia until the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he studied regional politics and local elites.
A journalist at a major national media outlet who covered national and regional politics in the 1990s calls Kynev “the best expert on regional politics in all of post-Soviet history” and “someone who knew practically everything about the political systems of Russia’s regions.” Andrey Buzin, a former co-chair of Golos, agrees. “Some people will go down in history because future generations will cite their work, regardless of what else can be said about their lives or personalities,” Buzin says, alluding to Kynev’s temperament.
Kynev also taught political science at the Higher School of Economics, starting in the 2000s and continuing until 2019. In 2012, he began working with the Committee of Civil Initiatives, which former Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Kudrin founded after the Bolotnaya Square protests.
An acquaintance of Kudrin’s tells Meduza that the former deputy prime minister tried to bring “the most capable specialists” into the committee, including political scientist Dmitry Oreshkin, Novaya Gazeta journalist Andrey Kolesnikov, economist Mikhail Dmitriev, and Kynev.
At the committee, Kynev continued to track Russian regional politics. He documented pressure on the opposition and on local elites who disagreed with those in power, and tracked election fraud.
Hi, I’m Katya.
I’ve been running Meduza’s crowdfunding since 2021. Today, supporting Meduza is a crime in Russia. You can be sent to prison just for donating. We’re still able to do our work thanks to thousands of our Russian readers who now live abroad. But even they’re no longer safe.
Imagine you’ve left Russia, but then your mom becomes seriously ill. It could be your last chance to see her, so of course you go home. At the border, you’re interrogated. Officers hack into your phone and search for any trace that you’ve donated to Meduza.
The Kremlin is counting on that fear, and it’s working. People are afraid to donate. I’m afraid for our supporters, because any one of them could end up in prison. And I’m afraid for Meduza. Without crowdfunding, we simply can’t continue. So if you live outside Russia and don’t have to worry that donating to Meduza could keep you from going home to your family, I’m asking for your help. Please support our work.
In 2018, Kynev became an expert with the Liberal Mission research foundation, which former Russian Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin founded in 2000 and which remains active. Speaking on the foundation’s behalf in 2021, Kynev criticized the State Duma election campaign for widespread fraud, including in remote electronic voting, and for mobilizing voters through their employers.
That year, Kynev also praised the New People party for the first time, saying it responded to a “genuine public demand for renewal of the political system.” He said, however, that he did not consider New People a full-fledged opposition party and that it had been created with the authorities’ approval. In 2023, he again praised the party’s work, calling its campaign “the most creative and eye-catching, geared more toward young people.” A year later, during Russia’s presidential election campaign, he called New People’s Vladislav Davankov “the standout” candidate.
“We need to keep some seeds of change and independent forces alive within the system so that something new might grow when a window of opportunity opens,” Kynev said of Davankov. The outlet Vestka reported that Kynev “unofficially collaborates” with New People.
Kynev stayed in Russia after the war began. An acquaintance tells Meduza that he did so on principle and to “stay in touch with the subject of his research — Russian regional politics itself.” “That mattered a lot to Sasha. He couldn’t see himself as a talking head abroad,” the acquaintance says.
Kynev nevertheless gave several interviews to journalists from opposition outlets. In a 2022 interview with Glasnaya, for example, he criticized some opposition figures for making radical statements about Russia and demoralizing Russians who had stayed in the country. He also said the mass departure of activists was weakening municipal election campaigns, which he called one of the few remaining ways for people to organize themselves.
In a 2023 interview with Radio Liberty, Kynev argued that “regional elites” no longer existed: 60% of governors came from outside the regions they governed, and major regional businesses had become branches of national companies. He said there could be “no dissenting faction” within the current system. In his view, change in the regions would come only after change in Moscow.
Kynev also regularly criticized Russian political émigrés, saying they were disconnected from the realities and concerns of life inside Russia. He likewise took aim at media outlets in exile, which he called “liberal-schizoid,” including for publishing stories about a possible new wave of mobilization after the September 2026 State Duma elections.
“Alexander’s tragedy is that his field of work [regional politics] was almost entirely destroyed, and he tried to prove otherwise,” says the journalist who covered Russian politics in the 1990s.
Kynev stayed in Russia even after Russia’s Justice Ministry added him to its “foreign agents” registry in February of this year.
Meduza has learned that Kynev was abroad shortly before the State Duma elections but returned specifically for the vote. “What does happiness look like in a Russian election? It’s when they haven’t stolen everything from you — though they could have,” he said with irony in a September 21 post. On the program “Zhivoy Gvozd” (“Live Nail”), Kynev said the authorities had “gone too far in using administrative pressure to drive turnout” during the elections — a reference to excessive employer-driven voter mobilization.
News of Kynev’s detention emerged on the afternoon of September 25. He faces a charge under a law that prohibits producing, selling, or shipping large quantities of drugs. The offense carries a prison sentence of 10 to 20 years.
Kynev’s lawyer, Mikhail Biryukov, says he is accused of attempting to sell a large quantity of drugs. Kynev denies the allegation, and the defense will appeal the detention order, Biryukov tells Meduza. He says his client is “holding up well.”
In his most recent Facebook post, on September 23, Kynev summed up his work during the election campaign:
I often had to play therapist to friends during this tense, nerve-racking campaign, constantly hearing things that often can’t be shared publicly. […] I need at least a little time to rest and take a mental break. So I’ll be posting a little less often for now. I need to recharge my batteries.

articles.title: Tens of thousands protest German conscription plans (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Tens of thousands protest German conscription plans (VIDEOS)
Tens of thousands of students took to the streets across Germany on Friday to protest the government’s military service reform amid Berlin’s push to expand the armed forces, citing the alleged threat from Russia.
Organizers of the “School Strike Against Conscription” said around 45,000 students joined demonstrations in some 100 cities and towns on Friday. Police did not provide a nationwide figure, but reported around 2,400 protesters in Berlin, while hundreds more rallied in Stuttgart, Nuremberg, Munich, and Hamburg.
Footage from the video agency Ruptly showed crowds marching through Hamburg carrying banners reading “We won’t fight in your wars,” “Education instead of bombs,” “Not our war” and “Russia is not our enemy.”
Some protesters also targeted Chancellor Friedrich Merz, with banners reading “No Merz, no war, no billionaires!”
🔥🪖 Schulstreik gegen Wehrpflicht 
Zahlreiche Schüler sind am Freitag erneut auf die Straße gegangen, um gegen eine mögliche Wehrpflicht zu demonstrieren. Wie die Initiative „Schulstreik gegen Wehrpflicht“ mitteilte, gab es bundesweit etwa 100 Demonstrationen. Pressesprecher… pic.twitter.com/xMTDFU8qBM
“I don’t want to see my child sent off to war by politicians like the ones we currently have in Germany,” one protester told Ruptly. She said she was “more afraid of [European Commission President] Ursula von der Leyen, Merz… than of any Russian president.”
A student described the reform as a “form of war preparation,” arguing that young people could eventually be forced “to shoot at young people… for the interests that aren’t ours… but the interests of profit-hungry arms corporations and politicians.”
Germany’s Military Service Modernization Act, which took effect in January, requires 18-year-old men to complete a questionnaire on their willingness and suitability for military service. Mandatory medical examinations for men born in 2008 or later are due to begin in July 2027. Service remains voluntary, but parliament can activate compulsory military service if recruitment targets are not met or the security situation deteriorates.
🇩🇪 In #Berlin skandieren die Demonstranten 
„Merz, leck Eier!“ 🔈💥
Die Schüler protestieren gegen die Wehrpflicht... pic.twitter.com/LFJESiCR8Q
The government aims to expand the Bundeswehr to more than 260,000 active troops and 200,000 reservists by 2035, citing Germany’s NATO commitments and what it describes as a worsening security environment in Europe.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has previously warned that Germany must be prepared for a potential conflict with Russia. Moscow has repeatedly rejected claims that it intends to attack NATO countries, describing them as “nonsense.”

articles.title: Ukraine strikes three Russian plants involved in missile production
articles.body:
Ukraine strikes three Russian plants involved in missile production
Ukraine's defence forces have struck three facilities in Russia's Ulyanovsk, Tula and Voronezh oblasts.
Source: The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
The targets included the Yefremov Synthetic Rubber Plant in the city of Yefremov, Tula Oblast, and Voronezhsintezkauchuk near Voronezh.
Details: The General Staff said both facilities are involved in the production of solid rocket fuel, including for ballistic missiles used by the Iskander operational-tactical missile system.
Another facility struck was NPP Zavod Iskra plant in Russia's Ulyanovsk. Ukrainska Pravda reported the attack earlier citing OSINT sources. The General Staff said the plant was struck on the night of 24-25 September.
The General Staff said Zavod Iskra is part of the Almaz-Antey air and missile defence conglomerate and produces semiconductor devices and electronic components for Russia's military-industrial complex.
The General Staff added that, as part of production cooperation, the plant is involved in manufacturing Kh-59M2/M2A guided air-launched missiles and the 72V6 combat vehicle used in the Pantsir-S surface-to-air missile and gun system and its variants.
The General Staff said Voronezh is around 180 km from the Ukrainian border, Yefremov about 300 km away and Ulyanovsk around 800 km away.
Background: It was reported earlier that Ukraine's defence forces attacked the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Russia's Samara Oblast. The plant supplies Russia's military-industrial complex with synthetic rubber, which, among other things, is used to produce solid rocket fuel for short-range and ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Trump asked Zelenskyy to meet with Putin in Moscow for peace talks - media
articles.body:
Trump asked Zelenskyy to meet with Putin in Moscow for peace talks - media
Kyiv • UNN
This week, the U.S. president again urged the Ukrainian leader to go to Moscow for a meeting with the Russian dictator. Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejected the proposal.
U.S. President Donald Trump again urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this week to travel to Moscow for a meeting with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin — despite repeated refusals in the past — as the United States seeks to revive peace talks between Ukraine and Russia, UNN reports, citing Bloomberg.
Details
The publication reports that Zelenskyy rejected the proposal, which was made during a meeting with the American leader at the UN. According to people familiar with the Ukrainian leader’s position, Trump’s raising the issue displeased him.
When journalists asked when he would visit Moscow, Zelenskyy replied: "On a missile," adding an obscene word.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
We would add
Russian dictator Vladimir Putin hinted at Russia’s readiness to consider peace proposals, but said it would first determine its own interests. He also threatened Kyiv with new strikes.

articles.title: Russia accuses Ukraine of attempting to disrupt elections with Western financial, intelligence support
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
Russia accused Ukraine on Friday of attempting to disrupt the Sept. 18-20 State Duma elections with financial, intelligence and technical support from Western countries.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said several election officials and civilians were killed and wounded in drone attacks during the voting period. She added that 41 people, including four children, were killed and 338 injured in the last week, accusing Ukraine of attacks on civilian infrastructure in Russia using weapons supplied by Western countries.
The ministry said attacks during voting mainly targeted polling stations, including schools, cultural centers and social and administrative facilities. It said more than 70 precincts and territorial election commission buildings were damaged by Ukrainian strikes.
Despite the “fierce external pressure,” it said Russian voters participated in the elections and demonstrated “resilience and unity.”
Russia also criticized Ukraine’s proposed 2027 budget, saying its $37.3 billion deficit reflected a sharp increase in defense spending.
Moscow claimed Ukraine planned to allocate about 43.8% of its gross domestic product to defense, with nearly half designated for weapons and military equipment.
The statement claimed Kyiv was relying on Western financial support to cover its budget deficit, including potential assistance from the European Union, G7 countries, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
Russia also criticized the recent meeting in Ukraine’s Ivano-Frankivsk region of the Carpathian Eight initiative on trade and security, comprising Austria, Hungary, Poland, Serbia, Slovakia, Romania, Ukraine and the Czech Republic.
Ukraine has not responded to the Russian claims, and independent verification remains difficult due to the ongoing war.
The head of the Russian Central Election Commission Ella Pamfilova said Friday that the ruling United Russia party secured 349 of 450 seats in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, in the legislative vote.

articles.title: Iran offers Trump deal before US election
articles.body:
Iran offers Trump deal before US election
Iran has offered the US a new deal aimed at ending the months-long conflict before the midterm election in November, directly challenging President Donald Trump’s claim that Tehran is deliberately waiting until after the election to reach an agreement.
Trump claimed in a speech at the UN on Tuesday that Iran is deliberately stalling the talks to see how Republicans perform in the November 3 midterm election, and predicted that Tehran would make a deal “right after” the vote. He also threatened to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic if negotiations fail.
“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told reporters on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday. “We wish Americans to return to the MOU before the midterms,” he said, referring to the memorandum of understanding reached by the US and Iran in June.
“We did reach an agreement with your president… The problem is that America, instead of conducting dialogue, descended into the arena by bombing us first, by blocking every pathway,” Pezeshkian said in an interview with Fox News. “We will stand resolutely to defend ourselves. We never sought war… It’s America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not.”
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran has submitted a proposal in which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within around a week and negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program rapidly resumed. The proposal was sent through mediators during talks in New York this week.
Under the plan, Tehran would restore navigation through the crucial oil shipping route in exchange for Washington lifting its economic blockade, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports, and releasing some frozen Iranian assets. Iran is also seeking an end to hostilities on other fronts, including Israel’s combat operations in Lebanon.
US and Iranian negotiators are discussing a phased arrangement in which the blockade and restrictions on Hormuz would be addressed first, Reuters reported, citing Iranian, regional, and Western diplomatic sources.
Tehran has not abandoned its claim to regulate Hormuz, with Iranian officials continuing to insist that the waterway should be managed by Iran and Oman and that fees should be charged for services provided to passing vessels.
Araghchi said the proposal largely follows the terms of the June memorandum rather than introducing new demands, adding that Iran is waiting for a response.
Araghchi has also held a series of meetings with foreign counterparts in New York, including Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Moscow has said there is “no alternative” to a diplomatic settlement of the crisis provoked by the “illegal actions” of the US and Israel.
The renewed diplomatic push comes amid mounting pressure on both sides. The US blockade has sharply restricted Iran’s oil exports, while Tehran’s controls over Hormuz have disrupted one of the world’s most important energy corridors and helped push oil prices above $100 a barrel and US diesel prices to historic highs.
Pezeshkian, who is the first foreign head of state to speak at the UN while his country is at war with the US, told the chamber on Wednesday that Tehran is prepared for “dialogue and diplomacy” but will not negotiate under threats of force and “will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”

articles.title: Putin says Russia will not attack Europe and blames Ukraine for the breakdown in peace talks
articles.body:
Putin says Russia will not attack Europe and blames Ukraine for the breakdown in peace talks
This is a brief summary of statements Vladimir Putin made to journalists on the sidelines of the United Cultures Forum in St. Petersburg. Their full meaning and context have been preserved, though some passages may have been edited or rearranged.
Shortly before the State Duma elections, Ukraine said it was ready to return to negotiations. Russia was prepared to resume contact after the elections. But on the main voting day, Kyiv attacked Moscow, launched more than 1,600 drones, and struck polling stations. After what they did, we’ll consider how to respond. We’ll decide whether to resume negotiations based on our own interests. Ukraine must feel the effects of Russia’s retaliatory strikes. The strikes are so destructive that Ukraine is raising the prospect of a ceasefire and trying to stop Russia’s “Geran” drone strikes. Kyiv’s provocations only make things worse for Ukraine. Russia is not preparing for military action against Europe; we have no such plans. European countries themselves are escalating tensions and engaging in provocations. They want to keep using Ukraine as a tool in their fight against Russia. We know that Russian speakers’ rights are being violated in the Baltic states, and we are responding with humanitarian measures.
